Social media has become a primary hub for social engagement, where online communities frequently share hate speech across diverse modalities. We introduce a new multi-modal dataset comprising tweets (text) and associated profile images for capturing instances of hate. The dataset includes both hate/non-hate classifications and further categorizes hate content into seven specific classes. Our proposed framework, UMMHI (Unobservable Multi-modal Hate-identifiction), leverages a dual-encoder architecture to extract features from the text and image components, which are then aggregated via a self-attention mechanism to generate the ultimate label. Notably, UMMHI offers interpretability by explicitly modeling the contributions of each modality to prediction accuracy. Experimental validation demonstrates that UMMHI achieves state-of-the-art performance on the proposed multi-modal dataset.

This study examines how varying degree distributions influence the synchronization behavior of large, randomly connected Type-I neuron networks subjected to Kramers escape. The Kramers escape model, previously utilized for isolated integrate-and-fire neurons, encapsulates the Type-I firing dynamics through three key parameters: resting membrane potential, firing threshold, and escape noise intensity. Our findings indicate that when Kramers escape occurs across all neurons, the mean first-passage time (mean FPT) for collective firing is determined by the network size and its degree distribution, whereas the variance in first-passage times remains independent of both structural configuration and neuron count. Furthermore, we explore scenarios where only a subset of neurons is capable of Kramers escape, revealing that such heterogeneous excitability can either suppress or promote synchronization depending on which specific neuron types constitute the majority.

Autotomic Program Repair (APR) seeks to automatically locate, fix, and verify bug patches without human input. A leading approach within this domain is patch creation using antagonistic examples, a method that relies on failing test cases to guide the transformation of candidate fixes toward failure. However, generating antagonistic examples is not always feasible because faulty input-output pairs may be inaccessible for certain programs. This study introduces a novel antagonistic patch creation method that operates effectively regardless of the program's specific type. Rather than utilizing test cases, our technique constructs antagonistic inputs by inverting the binary or character encoding of input strings. This study demonstrates the application of our approach on 126 bugs from the Great AP-RE dataset, yielding successful resolutions in 10 cases.

This work introduces a novel framework based on data spectrum analysis to investigate the capability region of Gaussian input-dependent fixed gain communication channels (GIFC). The approach models the GIFC channel as an additive noise channel featuring a non-uniform power spectral density (PSD) constraint. We demonstrate that the capacity of this equivalent channel defines a lower bound on the GIFC capability. This bound becomes exact whenever the additive noise follows a Gaussian distribution with unitary PSD; in such a scenario, the spectrum of the input-output signal expands to cover the entire non-negative real axis. Furthermore, we outline a numerical procedure for determining the optimal PSD for both input signals and additive noise that achieves that bound. This optimal distribution concentrates over a finite segment of the non-negative real axis and results in the input signal sharing the same spectral shape as the channel's additive noise.

The 3D Flow Examination (3D-FE) represents an innovative instrument designed to analyze the collision architecture and the equation of state by utilizing three orthogonal beams. This approach creates three distinct reaction zones to facilitate flow measurements along all three dimensions. This 3D configuration offers unique advantages, including the capacity to measure collision parameters from varied perspectives and the ability to determine particle yields without needing to know initial participant counts. Additionally, by employing three beams of varying particle types, it enables the exploration of charge-dependent collective movement, also known as isospin transport. The feasibility of 3D-FE has been verified through numerical simulations using a Boltzmann-Triggering-Nuclear Transport Model (Boltz-NNM). These simulations demonstrate that the method can effectively reproduce key observables such as transverse momentum distributions, flow coefficients, elliptic asymmetry, and isotropic charge ratios.

The rapid emergence of COVID-19 has precipitated a global crisis, necessitating immediate intervention. While contact tracing is the primary defense against infectious diseases, it is often insufficient to curb the virus's spread. Consequently, there is a critical need for a more effective strategy to identify and isolate infected individuals before they can transmit the disease. We introduce a novel method utilizing deep learning to analyze social media content for the early detection of the pandemic. A significant challenge with this approach is the latency between infection and the appearance of associated online discussions. We propose a new adversarial training framework designed to identify COVID-19 mentions appearing shortly after an infection occurs. This system is further enhanced by a mechanism that extracts privacy-preserving mentions, such as anonymized names, from the data. We validate the system's efficacy using social media data collected during the pandemic, demonstrating its potential to facilitate timely identification of cases and, consequently, effective prevention of the disease's further transmission.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential for analyzing graph-structured data, yet training and deploying them demands substantial computational resources. In scenarios involving large graphs, centralized approaches often fail due to the prohibitive costs of gathering data and model parameters at a single point. To address this, we introduce a framework for wirelessly enabling distributed GGN deployment, presenting an innovative system where transmission and network intelligence are tightly integrated. Our solution leverages cooperative non-orthogonal multiple access (C-NOMA) to allow users to share their computational results, ensuring that those with stronger communication links shoulder a larger portion of the computation to assist others. This creates a cooperative trade-off between wireless transmission and computational load, optimizing the overall process. The study mathematically formulates the minimum total communication-load objective and derives the optimal centralized solution using dynamic programming, alongside a near-optimal distributed algorithm. Simulations confirm that our proposed scheme achieves performance close to optimal while demonstrating that cognitive cooperation within the network significantly enhances the efficiency of both the communication links and the computation tasks.

Homicides are a prevalent form of violence in Brazil, particularly within the province of Goias, which recorded 10,000 cases in 2014. This study examines spatial patterns in homicide rates across Goias's municipalities between 2002 and 2014, identifying a significant increase in both the spatial clustering of incidents and the overall correlation between neighboring towns. While spatial lag models suggest that local homicide rates are influenced by local and regional economic and social factors, the distinct observation of spatially autocoragated residuals from these models indicates that unaccounted-for variables continue to influence crime distribution.

This study introduces a novel algorithm, designated as issue-aware stochastic gradient descent (IW-SGD), which leverages the inherent structure of the loss landscape to enhance training efficiency. The approach involves two primary modifications: first, the computation incorporates higher-order derivatives to refine gradient estimates, and second, the update rule dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on the specific characteristics of the loss landscape. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this method offers superior convergence rates compared to both standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and higher-order adaptive methods. Extensive experiments on various machine learning tasks validate these findings, confirming that IW-SGD consistently outperforms established baselines such as standard SGD and Adam in both accuracy and speed.

IAXO, the proposed large-scale neutrino detector, is currently being developed to resolve the solar neutrino problem. Its initial configuration, designated BabyIAXO, is designed to validate the instrument's feasibility by conducting a pilot experiment. This paper explores the potential for BabyIAXO to image the Sun's core, focusing on the temperature-dependent gradient inherent to core conditions and its impact on temperature and heat flux distribution. By analyzing these factors, we can study the thermal and hydrodynamic processes occurring in the Sun's interior. The analysis reveals that core imaging via the Sun is viable with both versions of the detector, though the analysis method must be adapted based on whether the Sun's temperature gradient is assumed to be constant or variable.

This paper introduces a new category of self-exciting systems characterized by a specific approach to defining the right-hand side differential equation via a left eigenvector of a non-Hermitian matrix. Although the strategy mirrors that used for two excitation models, the resulting system exhibits distinct features, most notably a complex limit cycle. Within the linear regime, the system displays a complete set of unstable modes, while the nonlinear dynamics are marked by a Hopf bifurcation that generates this complex limit cycle. Furthermore, the steady state demonstrates a unique stability regime where it remains stable despite the system comprising an unstable number of modes. At the transition to instability, the limit cycle emerges, and the dynamics become those typical of a subcritical Hopf bifurcation, resulting in the coexistence of both a stable steady state and a stable, periodic complex limit cycle.

We introduce DexGraspNet, an extensive dataset comprising 65,625 dexterous grasps across 6,515 diverse objects. A unique characteristic of this work is the inclusion of multiple grasps per object to enhance the training of grasping networks. To efficiently annotate such a large volume, we leveraged the fact that generation of simulated grasps is rapid and accurate, allowing us to create a robust benchmark for evaluating dexterous grasp dexterity. By comparing various dexterity metrics, we demonstrate that our proposed method for computing grasp dexterity is both effective and efficient. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these annotations produce reliable training results for dexterous grasping networks. Empirical evaluations confirm that trained models generalize exceptionally well to unseen objects, achieving a mean dexterity score of 0.65 on the test set.

Respiration-induced motion is a primary obstacle to the real-time, free-breathing MRI of the abdomen and thorax. This study introduces a motion-compensated four-dimensional (4D, or 3D plus respiratory motion) T2-weighted in-plane spin-echo sequence. The method applies motion correction in the phase-encoding (RE) dimension, utilizing a reference scan and a motion-encoding gradient orthogonal to the reference. Motion is estimated by comparing phase shifts between the two datasets. A reference scan with a long repetition time (TR) and turbo factor (TF) of 10 is used to generate a motion-compensated scan with a shorter TR and higher TF of 20. This approach halves the total scan time while maintaining a high turbo factor. Experimental data from 10 healthy volunteers (n=10) were analyzed using a 3 Tesla scanner with a high acceleration factor of 10. The resulting images displayed high quality, with no detectable motion artifacts. The study concludes that 4D motion-corrected T2-weighted imaging is a viable strategy for free-breathing abdominal and thoracic scanning.

Model compression is essential for deploying AI systems in resource-constrained environments. Current approaches typically shrink model dimensions or prune weights, often resulting in a loss of accuracy due to the disruption of data flow. We present InDistill, a framework utilizing knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from a large source model to a compact target architecture. By formulating knowledge distillation as an optimization problem, we preserve the target model's data flow to create a more efficient architecture with enhanced performance. We evaluate our approach on a variety of CNN and Transformer architectures within Image classification and text generation contexts. The results demonstrate that InDistill surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in compressing Vision Transformers and image-classification CNNs, while also generating lighter-weight language models that require less memory and fewer computational operations for text generation.

Topological similarities of the plane are homeomorphisms that transform level sets of a submersion function into topologically equivalent submersion functions. This work focuses on the plane's topological similarities concerning a specific class of submersion functions characterized as "linear-like." Specifically, a submersion function $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is deemed linear-like if its regular level sets are smooth curves that behave like lines at both positive and negative infinity; in this context, these lines may either be parallel or share common limits at one or both ends. We establish that the group of topologic similarities of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with respect to linear-like functions is structurally identical to the group of topologic similarities of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with respect to the foliations generated by these functions. Additionally, we demonstrate that two foliations on $\mathbb{R}^2$, each possessing a topological structure composed of a fibration over an interval with fibers as open intervals, are topologically equivalent if and only if they admit a submersion function that is linear-like.

The escalating threat of biodiversity loss and the challenges posed by a growing global population necessitate a deep understanding of how human activities influence dry-land ecosystems. This study integrates historical records with the ED2-dyn vegetation dynamics model to simulate the co-evolution of plants and herbivores across North American dry-lands from 1850 to 2000. Our analysis reveals that livestock in non-residential grazing zones significantly reduce plant biomass, alter species composition, and decrease the carbon sink capacity of dry-land vegetation. These adverse effects are most pronounced in semi-arid environments characterized by high seasonal precipitation variability. The findings underscore the critical need for further research into how distinct management practices shape plant communities in dry-land regions worldwide.

The initial results regarding CountSketch's ability to handle adaptive data were surprisingly encouraging, suggesting it could match the performance of the full data matrix even when processed sequentially based on previous observations. However, a closer examination reveals that this phenomenon stems from the fact that adaptive data, under these conditions, is effectively limited to a very low rank. This paper investigates how much the performance of such a low-rank component must be compressed, demonstrating that CountSketch is indeed sufficiently effective. We further establish that the number of required samples is nearly optimal by providing matching lower bounds for specific cases, which also apply to the related MatrixSketch and to matrix inversion using the Nystr\"om method. Additionally, we explore the performance of CountSketch on the full set of samples rather than just the selected subset. In this context, we identify that the probability of error for the solution is governed by the \emph{stable rank} of the underlying matrix. We also examine how CountSketch behaves specifically with respect to the spectral gap.

We introduce ipie, a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) package that delivers both flexibility and efficiency across CPU and GPU environments. The software features a custom-designed AFQMC implementation that leverages Green's function restrictions and employs linear equation solvers optimized for multithreaded parallel computing. To ensure efficient GPU utilization, ipie employs efficient transfer protocols and optimized memory management strategies. We have evaluated the performance of ipie using diverse electronic systems spanning atoms, molecules, and solids. The software's efficiency is further demonstrated by its ability to execute calculations that rival those of established Monte Carlo programs.

A major hurdle in modern finance involves reaching consensus on complex topics like trade confirmations and reconcilings, a process that is both costly and slow. This process requires mutual agreement on intricate details involving numerous participants, often necessitating repeated manual interventions. This study proposes a quantum-based system designed to expedite multi-party consensus, particularly within the domain of high-frequency trading. By leveraging the capabilities of the quantum cloud, this system utilizes a modified version of the Prisoner's Dilemma to drive collaboration among parties. This approach ensures that a cooperative, winning outcome is reached efficiently, even if some parties are prone to opportunistic, non-cooperative strategies.

We investigate how to maximize revenue for a service provider offering a specific item to a population of customers, considering the impact of both brokers and a limited budget for marketing. Customers only purchase the service if their net utility is positive; however, their purchase probability increases with the service's intrinsic value. Conversely, the presence of brokers—who buy the item from the provider at a discounted rate and resell it at a markup for a commission—reduces this demand. The study focuses on two primary questions: first, determining the optimal pricing strategy to maximize income when customer types and their proportions are unknown, given certain constraints on broker supply and margins; second, developing an online pricing mechanism that performs well even when the types and proportions of customers are not known in advance. The proposed solution guarantees a minimum level of competitive ratio and provides a formal analysis of this guarantee under various conditions.

This work presents a method to generate abstractive condensation summaries using a non-semantic plan. We begin by automatically creating a list of entity names serving as the condition inputs for summarization. Subsequently, a generative model creates sentences referencing these entities in the order dictated by the plan, producing the final condensed result. To evaluate this approach, we developed a planning system capable of constructing meaningful entity sequences. Empirical evaluations show this plan-based approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art transformer-based generative models. Additionally, we demonstrate that planning facilitates improved human interpretability of the summaries and allows for easier incorporation of external knowledge during generation.

This study establishes conditions for the differentiability of a multivariate real-valued function $nDf(X)$, leveraging the known differentiability of its $(n-1)Df$ counterpart. Sufficient criteria for this property are formulated through requirements on both the traditional and generalized Jacobian matrices of the lower-dimensional function. Furthermore, by applying these results, we derive an adequate standard ensuring the differentiability of convex functions. Our methodology extends previous research conducted by Li and by Mordukhovich and Shao.

Vocal entrainment, the phenomenon where speakers subtly mimic each other's speech patterns, serves as a critical mechanism for social connection and communication. However, because these vocal adjustments occur rapidly and respond to the immediate context, isolating and measuring them in real-time dialogue remains difficult. This study introduces a new approach to measuring vocal entrainment in head-to-tail interactions, leveraging audio from 120 dialogues between people with schizophrenia and healthy participants. The system extracts vocal features and contextual data, then applies a contextual-sensitive algorithm to evaluate the degree of vocal synchronization. The findings indicate that the approach successfully detects entrainment dynamics in real-time dialogue and achieves statistical significance. The study also reveals that both healthy individuals and patients with schizophrenia engage in vocal entrainment, though the latter show reduced levels of vocal clarity. The study also shows that people with schizophrenia show a lower degree of vocal clarity and that the approach is effective in measuring the vocal clarity and the vocal clarity of people with schizophrenia.

We present an overview of the VET-Alpha project, a pioneering initiative utilizing the VLT-MUSE instrument to observe a burst-mode disk galaxy (NGC 6052) in the Hubble deep field. This galaxy serves as a key laboratory for investigating the regulation of star formation by outflows, a process expected to be critical in high-surface-brightness galaxies. By leveraging MUSE's exceptional capabilities, this study offers detailed spatially resolved data on both ionized gas and stellar populations. Our findings reveal that star formation is occurring at a rate of 0.034 ± 0.004 solar masses per solar year, with a star-formation efficiency of 0.034 ± 0.001 per 100 million years. These metrics indicate that NGC 6052 is currently undergoing a vigorous burst of star formation. Furthermore, the galaxy's current star formation rate is nearly an order of magnitude higher than its long-term average, suggesting that NGC 6052 is nearing a point where star formation will diminish significantly.

This paper introduces a new concept of "Simultaneous Robotic Structure" (SimRoSt), a significant extension of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) that integrates multiple robots and the physical environment they traverse or construct. Unlike traditional frameworks, the generalization of internal states involves three additional components: the configuration of the multibody robotic system, the spatial map of the surroundings, and the dynamics of the environment. Consequently, the standard SLAM state vector is augmented by generalized coordinates and momenta for the connected bodies representing the robots, while their movement adheres to holonomic and nonholonomic constraints. This expansion significantly complicates the state estimation process and graph optimization typical of current 2D and 3D SLAM. To address this, the work outlines a simultaneous estimation approach for multibody systems and their environments, utilizing a state-of-the-art feature-based algorithm. The methodology is demonstrated through a simulated scenario involving multiple robotic walkers and their surrounding structures.

We investigate the utility of self-supervised pre-training by introducing a new task, monocular depth assessment, and comparing its efficacy against standard classification tasks. Our analysis reveals that this new approach offers superior benefits for downstream semantic segmentation compared to classification tasks alone. Furthermore, we propose a streamlined two-view method to leverage pre-trained models for enhanced monocular depth assessment performance. The entire framework is implemented in an entirely self-supervised framework, and the code and models can be found at https://github.com/MADE-LAB/DEPTH4ALL

Calculating Kendall's $\tau$ and its variants is often computationally prohibitive for massive datasets, a limitation that our proposed methods address by reducing the data through the selection of strategic subsets, or "effective" samples. These subsets enable the rapid computation of Kendall's $\tau$, and the methodology can be refined via multiple acceleration strategies, including method-specific and general sample selection, quantization, and sampling-based approaches. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the resulting estimators are consistent and supports the approach with a range of numerical examples. Furthermore, the paper introduces and evaluates new speed-enhancing techniques tailored to subsets chosen based on the quantization or sampling of the original data.

Vehicular networks are increasingly vital for enabling intelligent transportation and autonomous driving. While Edge Intelligence (EI) has emerged as a promising paradigm to enhance these networks, privacy remains a critical challenge. This work introduces a unified framework that simultaneously addresses privacy concerns and supports EI functions within vehicular environments. The proposed framework empowers vehicles to perform data analysis and access resources on trusted edge servers, thereby ensuring data confidentiality and shielding user identities. Specifically, it allows for the protection of sensitive information during computation while enabling users to query and control their data usage. The authors demonstrate the practicality of this framework by implementing techniques such as Secure Multi-Party Computation and Trusted Execution Environment to facilitate privacy-aware EI. The paper further illustrates its real-world applicability through a use case focused on real-time traffic monitoring, highlighting the potential for dynamic traffic analysis while maintaining strict privacy safeguards.

This research investigates the system's equilibria, stability, and asymptotic behavior, analyzing how the ratio of the Allee effect's half-saturation constant to the predator's half-saturation constant influences the model's behavior. In this study, we investigate the on-line aspect pivot method (AP) within the framework of the primal-dual linear programming algorithm. By extending arguments from Grigoriev and Karpinski's work on the permutation cycle method, we demonstrate that the AP iteration sequence can be governed by at most $O(n^2)$ constraints, where $n$ denotes the total count of problem constraints.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with a unity element $1 \geq 1$. By applying a degree grading to $R$, we obtain $R=\bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} R_i$. We examine the group of units $R^\times$ within this ring structure and consider the normal subgroup of elements with degree zero: $R_0^\times$. When $R_0 = k$, where $k$ is a field, this subgroup $R_0^\times$ coincides with $k^\times$. In this paper, we investigate the first algebraic K-theory group $NK_1(R)$ specifically for such graded rings and derive a short exact sequence that defines this group.

This study examines the influence of off-shell virtualities on one-loop corrections for the differential cross-section associated with $pp \to t\bar{t}j$. By employing the renormalization group method within perturbative QCD, the calculation determines the differential cross-section simultaneously at both fixed and scale-dependent orders of the perturbative expansion. Findings indicate that off-shell effects introduce a relative shift of approximately 1% in the fully differential cross-section. Furthermore, these findings significantly influence the precision with which the top quark mass can be extracted from experimental data.

The rapid evolution of face recognition algorithms has spurred significant interest in face countermeasures against such systems. However, while literature has extensively covered detection methods for training data attacks, real templates, and deepfakes, the efficiency of vision transformers (ViTs) in handling zero-shot template attacks remains underexplored. This study investigates the zero-shot template attack within a framework of mutually efficient model architecture, specifically examining how ViTs perform. Experiments were conducted using ResNet101, SeNet154, and a pre-trained ResNet101 as the victim models, utilizing the CASIA-WebFace and CelebA datasets for attack generation. Results indicate that while the efficientap-ViT achieves higher robustness than ResNet154 and CENet, it remains less resistant than standard ViTs. Consequently, the research concludes that vision transformers are less effective for mitigating zero-shot template attacks compared to CNNs, highlighting a need for greater research focus in this area.

This paper introduces a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture designed to emulate the role of an autonomous vehicle. Specifically, the vehicle operates by executing actions in response to a specific driving environment. The model is trained on a simplified grid-based representation of roads, where the agent must navigate through defined cells. Within this framework, the agent's possible actions include moving forward, turning, or remaining stationary. The objective is to reach a designated target zone while optimizing for the shortest path and lowest energy consumption. We employ the Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithm to facilitate learning within this task environment. The research demonstrates that the DRL agent successfully acquires the necessary skills to navigate effectively, avoiding simulated obstacles and successfully reaching the goal area.

Asynchronous parallel multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (AP-MO-EAs) are popular choices for solving multi-objective problems (MOPs) due to their efficiency in resource management and high performance. However, their evaluation strategy introduces an evaluation-time bias that skews selection outcomes. This bias favors individuals with shorter evaluation durations, leading to an over-representation of their offspring in the population and the potential neglect of those with longer processing times. This study introduces a novel parent selection approach designed to mitigate such bias. By reducing the impact of varying evaluation times, the proposed method ensures a more balanced selection process. Experimental results using two AP-MO-EAs under this new selection mechanism confirm its effectiveness in reducing bias and improving overall performance across multiple performance indicators.

This study confirms the status of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb as a frigid super-Earth planet. By analyzing OGLE microlensing data collected with the Kepler telescope, the authors derive the host star's distance and velocity, alongside the orbit and mass of the forming planet. They note that the planet's orbit is highly eccentric, and the host star is a cold, low-mass star located approximately 10 parsecs away. To refine the planet's mass measurement, they utilized high-resolution near-infrared adaptive optics images obtained with the Keck telescope. This analysis revealed a secondary source in the microlensing event, attributable to the planet. Their findings indicate a planet mass between 1.6 and 2.0 Earth masses ($1.6-2.0 M_{\oplus}$) within a 95% confidence interval, with the most probable mass estimated at $1.8 \pm 0.2 M_{\oplus}$. They also provide a comprehensive analysis of the planet's thermal characteristics, noting that with an effective temperature of $170 \pm 10$ K, it represents the coldest super-Earth identified to date.

In contemporary science and engineering, numerous physical systems exhibit rapid oscillations driven by external fields, requiring their infinitesimal generators to be modeled as time-dependent Lindblad generators. To address the dynamics governed by these fast oscillators, various theoretical frameworks have emerged. However, an often-overlooked alternative is a classical Taylor series expansion based on the assumption that a distinct scaling parameter exists. We demonstrate that this series can indeed serve as a powerful tool for characterizing the dynamics of oscilloling autonomous quantum generators. By establishing a scaling parameter for the Lindblad generator, we show it functions as a fundamental parameter and utilize its associated Taylor expansion to construct effective Hamiltonians capable of describing the system's motion. Specifically, we derive closed-form expressions for the first- and second-order terms corresponding to this expansion.

This proposed mechanism of spin self-lattice formation is further supported by the detection of long-wavelength excitations.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become essential for machine learning tasks involving graph-structured data, yet their current training pipelines are constrained by slow, non-differentiable neighbor aggregation mechanisms and inefficient memory usage. Although recent efforts have optimized GNN inference, they fail to address these training bottlenecks. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a graph deep learning engine that offers both high-performance inference and streamlined training for GNNs. Our approach eliminates the non-differentiable aggregation step during training and boosts computational speed by leveraging modern multi-core and multi-GPU architectures. We validate this engine on several well-known benchmarks, including Cora, DBLP, and WikiFS. Experimental results demonstrate that our engine surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions by up to 10x in terms of inference latency and reduces training time by a factor of 2.5.

Legennd Memory Module (LMM) represents an effective mechanism for long-term sequence modeling by employing compresssed versions of the self-attention weights to store and retrieve information. Although LMM demonstrates competitive performance against state-of-the-art models while maintaining computational efficiency at runtime, its training remains serial due to the lack of a parallel algorithm. This paper presents a novel strategy to enable the parallelization of LMM training. The approach involves treating the convolution operation within the module as a sparse matrix multiplication, where sparse vectors represent a subset of the Legendre coefficients. By integrating existing sparse multiplication techniques into the training process, this method achieves significant speedups that scale effectively across multiple GPUs. The results demonstrate that the speed of training can be improved by a factor of $O(p)$, where $p$ represents the number of available GPU units.

Weakly-Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) have been the primary focus of dark matter research for several decades, prompting the widespread distribution of a vast array of detectors. Nevertheless, existing experimental results have consistently yielded null outcomes, suggesting a need to reassess the paradigm. This situation has driven the scientific community to advocate for weakly-interacting particles characterized by cross-sections significantly lower than the traditional WIMP scale. This overview examines the principal motivations for pursuing such particles and details the various experimental strategies, which are organized according to the relevant mass ranges.

This study introduces a naming convention model where language users migrate between communities, serving to explore the formation of naming inconsistencies across different groups and the conditions under which name re-orthogonalization occurs. The findings indicate that the level of inter-community interaction significantly impacts this heterogeneity in naming nomenclatures. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that even minimal migration is sufficient to sustain communication between the groups, despite the presence of variations in their names.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have established themselves as a potent tool for resolving various types of partial differential equations (PDPs), especially when those equations are expressed as weak forms. However, PINNs often struggle with "spectral bias," a phenomenon where models struggle to capture high-frequency details, and they are highly sensitive to hyperparameters. To address spectral bias, this study investigates the effect of optimizing PINNs in their momentum form versus a standard formulation. The optimization landscape of the momentum-based version is compared with the classical approach, with the spectral bias issue examined across both the half-Laplacian Helmholtz equation and the Navier-Stokes equations. The investigation includes a detailed analysis of the impact of the learning rate and momentum coefficient on the model's performance. The findings indicate that the momentum formulation offers faster training speeds and enhanced robustness to hyperparameter selection. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis suggests that employing PINNs with momentum can significantly lessen the impact of spectral bias.

This study examines the interaction of two elastic waves traveling through a viscously attenuated elastic medium. The findings indicate that if attenuation follows the Kelvin-Voigt model, stability conditions comparable to those in an unattenuated medium apply, provided they are met locally for the attenuation coefficients. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that within a half-space context, both wave modes exhibit stability regardless of attenuation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant potential for automating complex tasks across various domains, yet its opaque nature and difficulty in generating human-understandable explanations restrict its practical deployment. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical explanation framework that leverages Model-Based RL to produce concise, high-level descriptions justifying an agent's decisions. Specifically, our approach employs a novel explanation mechanism based on the Model-driven RL paradigm, where a knowledge graph is constructed to encode the agent's actions and policies alongside environmental dynamics. Building on this, a explanation agent utilizes inductive logic programming to derive hierarchical rules that clarify the agency's low-level decisions through high-level strategic reasoning. We validate this approach in both classical and modern RL environments, demonstrating that it successfully provides robust explanations while simultaneously enhancing sample efficiency.

We introduce a mechanism for optical irreversibility driven by quantum compression. This process utilizes an auxiliary two-level system (TLS) to couple left and right circularly polarized light modes through non-reciprocal rotation, thereby generating chiral states within the path-degree of freedom of the radiation field. By engaging the auxiliary system in a specific quantum state, the non-linearity of the device is established. Consequently, the resulting system defies detailed balance, yielding non-equilibrium optical transport characteristics that violate reciprocity.

The classical minimax problems posed by Fenton and Lutz involve finding the optimal placement of amplitude or phase delays for a specified delay spread to maximize the probability of exceeding a fixed signal threshold. This discussion examines a variant of these problems, termed "minimaxes of a Fenton type," which concern the inefficient, passive sensing of a single target at an unknown range. These problems, which are functions of the delay spread, take the form of "sum of translates," exemplified by functions such as $f(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n)=\sum_{i=1}^n\exp(-\tau_i^2/\sigma^2)$ and $f(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n)=\sum_{i=1}^n\exp(-|\tau_i|)$. These specific cases are analyzed, and it is demonstrated that they all share a common analytical structure. Furthermore, this study explores an extended scenario where the delay values are restricted to a bounded interval rather than being unconstrained.

Blind image restoration (BIR) is a critical area of research with extensive practical applications, though it remains a challenging inverse problem due to the inherent ill-posed nature of restoring corrupted images. This study introduces a novel Blind Image Restoration (BlIR) framework based on a kernel mixture model. The framework consists of two primary components: a kernel mixing module and a blind kernel unmixing module. To enhance the expressive power of these modules, a kernel mapping network is utilized for automatic kernel learning. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches, validating the model's effectiveness.

This paper explores nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equations and their connections to nonuniform pre-Lie and Liankative algebras through the nonuniform Yung-Baxter equations. We present a uniformization theorem that extends the original uniformization theorem for Yung-Baxter equations and examine various solutions, including those arising from councanonical and $S$-councanonical forms as well as commutative ones. Furthermore, we generalize both left and right (adjoint) actions associated with uniform Yung-Baxter equations in terms of nonuniform ones. Finally, we introduce a few new subvarieties linked to commutative and nonuniform Yung-Baxter equations.

The field of formal methods aims to ensure software reliability, particularly in safety-critical areas, by rigorously verifying that software adheres to its specifications. However, even within this formal setting, developers frequently encounter difficulties because the creation of meaningful and actionable specifications remains a major challenge. To address this, we propose a methodology for deriving these formal specifications from natural language inputs. Our approach involves two core components: (1) constructing a machine-readable natural language grammar capable of parsing program descriptions into semantically structured data, and (2) designing a semantics layer that maps programming constructs to program transformation operations. We have implemented this process using the C language and its corresponding Hoare logic, demonstrating that the resulting formal specifications successfully capture the original intent expressed in English. Finally, we execute validation processes to confirm that implementations align with their derived specifications.

This paper presents an enhanced version of Canopus, a highly available consensus protocol tailored for high-performance computing environments. While Canopus enables rapid agreement on values despite node crashes, we have further optimized it to tolerate node failures while addressing Byzantine errors, while simultaneously maintaining its performance efficiency. Our improvements include a mechanism to prevent double voting and a strategy to circumvent double counting. Additionally, we have designed a method to identify and handle node failures more effectively. Evaluation demonstrates that our new protocol, named RCanopus, achieves a 20% improvement in agreement speed compared to Canopus and provides robust protection against Byzantine errors, provided that less than one-third of the nodes are malicious.

Lateral lipid segregation and liquid-ordered domains within the bilayer are crucial for numerous cellular functions, a property largely driven by cholesterol. To better grasp how cholesterol influences membrane elasticity, we conducted bending modulus measurements on a multi-component system featuring cholesterol using an optical method. This approach involves tracking changes in the curvature-dependent surface polarizance of a membrane under applied bending forces. Our findings indicate that cholesterol enhances the bilayer's rigidity, revealing a progressive stiffening of a multi-component bilayer saturated with approximately 35% cholesterol up to roughly 10 times its initial modulus. This progression mirrors the emergence of liquid-ordered phases and aligns with previous nuclear magnetic resonance data. The optical technique offers a highly sensitive means to evaluate the rigidity of lipid membranes containing cholesterol.

In this work, we derive a completely new loop quantum astrophysical model by quantizing the ADM Hamiltonian, achieving a significant reduction in the resulting self-adjoint extension operator compared to previous approaches that utilized the Hamiltonian constraint.

The most energetic cosmic rays (ECRs) are extremely rare particles, and the recent surge in observations at the highest energies is a direct result of the extended operational timeline of the largest detectors, notably the Pierre Auger Observatory (PAO). This paper presents the most comprehensive catalog of the highest-energy cosmic rays detected to date, covering PAO's Phase I. We detail the characteristics of each event, analyze their spatial and temporal distributions, and evaluate potential correlations with solar and galactic magnetic fields, as well as the supergalactic coordinate system. Additionally, we examine the relationship between these events and ultra-high-energy cosmic rays sources, such as radio galaxies and quasars, identified from recent PAO studies. An updated version of this catalog can be accessed at: http://www.auger.ens.fr/ECCR/.

Recent advancements in deep object detection have produced models that achieve remarkable accuracy, yet their lack of interpretability and inability to quantify uncertainty are critical barriers to practical application. This study introduces a straightforward and effective approach to assessing uncertainty in object detectors. By treating the inference stage of a detector as an inference process for the target parameters of a Bayesian model, the method allows for uncertainty estimation through Monte Carlo Dropout within frameworks like Fast R-CNN and RetinaNet across various datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed technique yields competitive uncertainty assessments compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, outperforming contemporary approaches by 10%, the method significantly boosts confidence in high-quality predictions while suppressing uncertainty for low-confidence ones.

Accurate forecasting of traffic volume and congestion is vital for the efficient management of urban mobility and infrastructure. Accidents and poor maintenance further complicate traffic flow, making it necessary to address these variables alongside future traffic estimation. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging weakly supervised data to predict traffic volume and congestion across specific traffic segments. Unlike many existing methods that rely on the sparse output of trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for traffic image analysis, our strategy utilizes the strong, pre-trained CNN features directly. Specifically, we identify "traffic moving segments"—specific sub-regions within images that exhibit motion—to determine which areas are most critical for prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that predicting traffic conditions based on these identified moving segments yields superior accuracy compared to other approaches.

Following the work of Chiswell and Jechkov, we investigate rewriting systems within class $A_\infty$ (denoted as G), which consists of sentences asserting that infinitely many instances of a single predicate hold true. We introduce a set of reformulations representing the concepts equivalent to Noetherian and convergent rewriting systems specifically within this class $:\, these are termed "Gray classes." Additionally, utilizing these Gray-optimised rewriting mechanisms, I have derived the following: for any sentence $\phi$ belonging to $:\ G$, if $\phi$ is consistent, then there exists a sentence $\phi'$ within $\:\:G$ that is also consistent, equivalent to $\phi'$ in terms of logical validity, and possesses the structure of a Gray-class term. This stands as an original form of consistency reduction applicable to class $:\ : \infty$.

Epilepsy is a neurological condition defined by seizures, characterized by transient loss of consciousness or motor function. It is frequently associated with structural brain abnormalities, particularly within the hippocampus, which can be analyzed using MRI via the Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) technique. In this study, MRI images were processed to extract features using four distinct convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures. These images were then partitioned into non-overlapping sub-regions known as "instances." A decision tree model was employed to evaluate partitions based on CNN-derived features to generate a final classification output. The research findings indicate that CNN-based MIL is a highly effective approach for characterizing the hippocampus, and the CNN models trained on this technique demonstrate superior performance compared to conventional MIL approaches that rely on fixed handcrafted features.

We introduce an approach to study the pigeonhole phenomenon by utilizing the pigeonhole measure derived from mean transversal distance, applied to modes named after the birds and those representing available nest sites. Our findings indicate a near-complete mapping to the classical effect when addressing five pigeons with six labeled Nester, achieving a 95% factor, whereas the dynamic significantly diminishes at seven pigeons six. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the phenomenon can be effectively mapped through the quantum Fisher information and the amount of resource required to reach the pigeon state.

This study employs the SPSS-based Monte Carlo method to analyze cosmic ray particles (with energies exceeding 100 MeV) that reach low Earth orbit heights (300–2,000 km) during magnetic field events with indices (BZ) of -10 to -32 nT. The simulations account for magnetic rigidity between 0.5 GV and 4 GV, incorporating the Earth's geomagnetic field, atmospheric ionization, and particle capture mechanisms. The results indicate that the number of captured cosmic ray particles increases with both cosmic ray energy and altitude. Furthermore, the ratio of these captured particles to the primary flux of cosmic rays rises with energy up to approximately 4 GV before declining.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are increasingly vital for analyzing graph-structured data, yet their reliance on graph Laplacian-based message passing restricts them to a limited number of graph convolutional layers. This limitation stems from the inherent oversmoothing issue inherent in their design. To address this, we introduce a novel, dual-stage training architecture designed to overcome these barriers. Initially, we propose a pyramid-like shrinkage mechanism that mitigates oversmoothing by aggregating graph signals across nodes and edges at multiple scales. Subsequently, we address the degradation of graph topologies caused by shrinkage through a topology link reconfiguration strategy. This adaptive approach restructures the connections between graph units, restoring complex local patterns while preserving global shrinkage features. Empirical evaluations across diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our method substantially outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions in terms of both accuracy and robustness.

This work presents a new algorithm for obtaining a private low-rank matrix approximation, grounded in the Huber approach to solving robust statistics problems. The method is designed to satisfy the requirements of $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy. A key advantage of this algorithm is its efficiency, operating in time $O(N^3)$, where $N$ denotes the larger of the matrix dimensions. It achieves a rank of $O(\sqrt{1/w})$, with $w$ representing a parameter directly proportional to privacy requirements. By leveraging the Huber framework, the method can robustly recover a low-rank matrix even when the input matrix vector is subject to the corruption of an adversary. This capability allows the system to reliably estimate the true matrix from noisy data.

A unified physical framework is presented to characterize the extinction, emission, and polarization of sparsely populated interstellar dust. This model relies on the concept of "astrodust"—a unique particle type that combines the properties of classical interstellar dust grains with those of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). The proposed structure offers a streamlined, cohesive approach to analyzing how dust in this specific environment interacts with light.

In extremely low-mass stars (ELMSS) and brown dwarfs, the core pressure and temperature conditions limit the core accretion mechanism for giant planet formation, a mystery that persists despite recent discoveries of massive planets orbiting T-type subdwarfs. This study presents the detection of a massive, non-transiting exoplanet with a mass of $M_p = 1.6 \pm 0.2$ $M_{\rm Jup}$ orbiting the M5.5 $\pm$ 0.2 V M-dwarf CIDA 1 with a period of $P = 10.2 \pm 0.1$ days; its companion status is confirmed via radial velocity measurements. Using the star's age of approximately 1.1 Gyr, we estimate CIDA 1's mass to be $0.12 \pm 0.01$ M$_\odot$ and its radius as $0.18 \pm 0.02$ R$_\odot$, placing it firmly within the M-dwarf regime. This system marks the first known case of a massive planet orbiting a true M-dwarf. Furthermore, this pairing demonstrates that the gap between the minimum mass for starhood and the threshold for hosting a massive planet is remarkably narrow.

We investigate a four-cell variant of the classic Breadth-OUT game, a linear cellular automaton played on a graph where each vertex holds a black (on) or white (off) light. Selecting a specific vertex activates all its connected lights if they are off. Although the standard objective is to extinguish every light using the minimum number of moves, we introduce a novel challenge where players aim to maximize the total number of button presses. Using algebraic methods and computational analysis to examine all 256 possible initial configurations, we demonstrate that the game is solvable for every start state. Additionally, we have fully characterized the necessary and sufficient conditions, detailing the optimal move count and solution structure across all initial states.

This paper presents an image segmentation framework that integrates modern data-driven techniques with traditional variational modeling to enhance partitioning accuracy. A key innovation is a novel strategy for data-variational coupling that merges reinforcement learning with the level set method. This coupling mechanism identifies high-quality image partitions by maximizing the expected value of reinforcement signals derived from a policy network. The resulting optimization problem is solved using an augmented Lagrangian algorithm, which guarantees convergence to a stationary point. Furthermore, a dual-level architecture employs a segmentation network to initialize the level set method, significantly accelerating convergence. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, yielding improved segmentation performance.

Abstract Interpretation (AI) is a technique used to formally verify program properties, but its computational cost is often prohibitive. This paper introduces a method to reduce the complexity of specific sub-programs within a given global fixed point by utilizing an "unknown" variable to decouple their rising and falling phases. This decoupling process involves a computation-intensive operation performed only once during initialization, followed by significantly cheaper updates in subsequent steps. The decoupling algorithm is validated on both C and Java programs to demonstrate a reduction in both time and space complexity. The results indicate that the time performance of this decoupling approach is equivalent to that of standard fixed-point computation during the AI's rising phase.

Phonons serve as crucial carriers of thermal energy in non-metals, and the emergence of topological surface states in this context promises to facilitate energy transport free from backscattering. This study investigates the potential for manipulating the topology of the phonon band structure within piezoelectric ceramics through illumination. Specifically, we examine BaTiO₃ and Ba₀.₉Ca₀.₁TiO₃, revealing that the alteration of the phonon dynamical matrix driven by photo-induced temperature shifts results in the formation of both anomaly points and topological surface states. These findings offer new perspectives on the manipulation of topological phenomena in acoustic systems and open pathways for achieving anomalous, highly efficient elastic wave transport in functional materials.

Outlier detection is a critical and multifaceted challenge with broad applications in data mining, machine learning, and pattern recognition. In this paper, we introduce a novel data-driven approach for identifying outliers within metric spaces. Our method constructs a specific graph structure to facilitate the rapid and precise identification of anomalies. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposal surpasses existing outlier detection techniques in both efficiency and effectiveness.

This work investigates the spontaneous emission of an atomic emitter positioned near an ultra-slim metallic mirror, where its radiated electromagnetic field is significantly altered by mirror flexibility. Specifically, the mirror's mechanical response can cause atomic excitation, a process termed *back-excitation*. We analyze this phenomenon within the context of a cavity QED framework, modeling the mirror as a one-dimensional membrane. Extensive analysis of the coupling dynamics reveals that back-excitation scales with the atomic transition frequency and the magnitude of the dipole moment, demonstrating that this effect becomes substantial in the high excitation regime. We also map out the conditions under which this induced mechanical motion can trigger a cascade of atomic emissions. Additionally, we explore the reciprocal interaction, where the atom influences the mirror's dynamics, leading to significant mechanical acceleration. Finally, the text describes the complex pattern of electromagnetic waves generated by this mutual coupling between optical and mechanical systems.

Equity-based graph learning has recently gained prominence, though most current methods concentrate on fairness between pairs of nodes. This approach struggles to effectively capture node community structures, which are vital for fair employment practices, as it frequently treats small groups with identical characteristics as merely fair subsets. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of "community fairness" and develop a new learning framework designed to identify such groups and ensure they receive equitable treatment. Specifically, we develop a Convex Optimization formulation for achieving this fairness in the context of fair hiring within a graph setting where individuals are represented as vertices and affinity relations define the edges connecting them. Our proposed solution includes a specialized algorithm capable of processing the optimization model with a time complexity of $O(m \cdot \text{iter})$, where $m$ denotes the total number of edges and iter represents the number of iterations. Finally, we conduct comprehensive experiments demonstrating that our method outperforms baseline approaches by producing more accurate results regarding both fair hiring outcomes and the correct identification of fair subcommunities.

Enzyme kinetics are fundamental to biological systems, and their study often leverages iterative methods to extract kinetic parameters from experimental data. In this paper, we introduce a new analytical approach for reversionable enzyme kinetics by applying a specific iteration to the relevant kinetic differential equations. This technique yields successive approximations for a substrate's time-dependent concentration, as well as estimations for kinetic constants. Notably, the calculation of these approximations and constant estimations does not rely on the complete analytical resolution of kinetic differential equations; instead, it only utilizes initial data alongside measured outcomes from the kinetics experiments.

This paper reports on the search for natural and split supersymmetry scenarios at the LHC's 13 TeV proton-proton collider, focusing on events characterized by jets. The analysis leverages the transverse momentum of missing energy, defined as MET$_T$, which originates from neutral supersymmetric particles. The study examines datasets accumulated in 2016 and 2017, amounting to a combined integrated luminosity of 35.3 fb$^{-1}$. No events inconsistent with the background expectations were observed. The results are utilized to set new upper limits on the frequency of such events across various supersymmetry models. The most stringent constraints derived from these limits pertain to gaugino production scenarios yielding a minimum MET$_T$ of 100 GeV, specifically valid when the invariant mass of two leading jets remains below 1.3 TeV.

"Due to the unpredictable nature of financial markets, forecasting the timing and magnitude of market crashes is extremely difficult. Consequently, we developed a new methodology to identify when investors exhibit irrational expectations. This approach relies on the statistical analysis of event data to pinpoint anomalies in investor behavior. Specifically, we propose a probabilistic model for the termination of a bubble driven by a compound Poisson process with a random arrival rate that follows a Gamma distribution, resulting in an exponentially distributed mean time. This allows us to track how quickly investors adjust their expectations regarding the bubble's termination point. We demonstrate the utility of this model by revealing expectation-driven financial bubbles within the data of the Chinese and the US markets."

In this study, we investigate the ground state density profile $\rho(x)$ and energy spectrum $\mathcal{E}(n)$ of a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to constant external driving forces, employing the path integral formalism and Monte Carlo methods based on a Metropolis algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations were executed to determine how the characteristic energy levels and spatial density distributions vary in response to the driving force. Furthermore, we validate our numerical findings by comparing them against established analytical solutions.

Product reviews are abundant and serve as a primary source of information for assisting consumers in making informed purchasing decisions. However, the challenge of identifying a product that perfectly suits individual preferences remains difficult, particularly given the presence of numerous irrelevant or noisy entries within datasets. This study introduces a novel model, Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), designed for effective product recommendation through the intelligent integration of reviews. Affective analysis is central to SIFN's approach, as the model employs a dedicated sentiment analysis module to classify reviews into positive or negative categories. These predictions are then utilized by the fusion module, via gate mechanisms, to selectively retain sentiment-aligned information for each user while discarding unhelpful data. This process facilitates the generation of precise individualized recommendations. Experimental validation on three established review-based recommendation benchmarks demonstrates that SIFN significantly surpasses seven existing state-of-the-art methods in recommendation accuracy.

Code-switching (CS) creates challenges for Natural Language Processing by generating sentences that defy standard grammatical norms. While existing CS resources are abundant for low-resource languages, Arabic-English CS-specific resources remain scarce. To address this, we present a novel framework for augmenting Arabic-English CS data through lexical substitutions, which leverage parallel dictionaries to replace lexical items in the source language with alternative words. We assess this augmentation across individual lexical replacements as well as multi-word phrases. Our results indicate that choosing the most impactful words to replace significantly impacts data quality, with noun-noun substitutions proving more effective than mixing noun-verb pairs. Furthermore, our multi-word phrase augmentation strategy surpasses traditional single-word approaches in efficacy.

Relation Extraction (RE) aims to identify known relationships between entities within given text. This study introduces a novel framework leveraging knowledge graph link prediction to bolster RE. The framework consists of two phases: initially, Knowledge Graph (KG) Link Prediction enhances the probability distribution of potential entity pairs by identifying plausible connections; subsequently, this refined distribution is integrated into the RE model to augment performance. Empirical evaluations across three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant improvements. notably, the LKLPD model yields a 0.8% increase in F1 scores compared to the baseline knowledge-graph-enhanced RE model (LPG9).

This work introduces a method for calculating the timing characteristics of standard digital logic components, such as multiplexers, adders, and other basic elements. These figures are derived from unit-cell simulations, which utilize commercial Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools to obtain cell propagation and arrival times across various input vectors, resulting in a dataset of $n$ pairs comprising input vector data and corresponding propagation times. Using this information, a custom EDA tool applies its MatLab curve-fitting capabilities to determine the coefficients for polynomial models that represent delay based on vector index. These polynomials are subsequently refined by applying a "model merging" technique, which averages delay estimates across multiple input vectors to generate a single model for each unit cell type. The resulting approach offers a quick and effective means of modeling the delays for basic cells like MUXes and adders, which can then serve as building blocks to construct more complex model structures for advanced digital circuits.

Continuization is a widely adopted technique in reinforcement learning (RL) that enhances sample efficiency by broadening an agent's interaction with its environment. While previous research predominantly implemented this through a discrete grid-based framework, we introduce a general method for estimating Q-values in arbitrary metric spaces. This approach leverages the concept of "coarse-grained continuity," which asserts that Q-values for states within the same metric distance bucket are nearly identical. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that coarse-grained continuity holds for the optimal Q-function in infinite state spaces, assuming a finite collection of state features and applying the criterion that the expected reward and subsequent value are bounded within each feature bucket. We also establish that, within such spaces, the optimal policy remains invariant across states in the same bucket, and the optimal Q-function exhibits a unique, unbounded, and well-defined asymptotic behavior at the boundaries of these buckets. Based on these findings, we propose a methodology for determining metric spaces, calculating associated feature buckets, and deriving Q-values using asymptotic averages. We validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach through experiments on the Atari benchmark, comparing the experimental outcomes.

Understanding the neural mechanisms behind object perception is vital, yet it remains unclear how such a capability emerges from a visual system initially tuned to basic features. Previous research indicates that response to living versus non-living objects emerges early in the ventral visual stream (VVS), specifically within the anterior temporal lobe. This study utilized high-density EEG to examine how activation representing the distinction between animate and inanimate stimuli evolves throughout the entire VVS. Results demonstrate consistent localization of this animacy processing within the anterior VVS across participants. Furthermore, we found that this processing is driven primarily by differences in living versus non-living object representations rather than variations in overall stimulus strength. These findings offer high-resolution temporal confirmation of earlier spatial-based fMRI evidence.
