Ramanujan's theorem regarding odd zeta values is presented through a rational relation between Ramanujan's Hurwitz zeta function and its derivative, a relationship derived from corresponding properties of Bernoulli functions and their derivatives. A comparable theorem for odd ζ(2k+1) utilizing a hybrid between Bernoulli and Euler functions, also based on the calculus of these functions and their derivatives, is provided, with additional discussion extending the study to other families and addressing odd zeta values through generalized Bernoulli functions.

We introduce an equivariant elliptic cohomology theory that extends to spaces possessing only a circular group of non-isotropic action, applying specifically to non-isotropic $CP(V)$. By establishing an equivariant Borel-type transition formula for elliptic cohomology, we can explicitly calculate these values for the complex sphere $S^{2n+1}$. Using this framework to derive a closed-form solution, we compute an circle-invariant elliptic characteristic class for CP(V). This class is pointwise non-isotropic and functions analogously to a total Pontryagin class; its pointwise restriction to the Grassmann space of isomorphic CP(k,V) segments yields the generalized Pontryagin classes of those subspaces. The general theory is applied specifically here to the cases of $CP(2)$ and $CP(3)$. The original work is based on the paper "Equivariant Elliptic Homology for Actions of the Group Z_p^m" by the same author.

This research explores the domain of "algebraic topology within machine learning," known as MLTA, and investigates its potential to enhance machine learning methodologies through the integration of topological principles. It further identifies several current research directions in MLTA that hold particular relevance for physics and proposes strategies for applying these techniques to real-world physical challenges.

Using the nonrelativistic quantum electrodietd (NRQED) QCD framework, we investigate the angular distributions of $J/\psi$ within the $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c,\chi_{cJ}$ ($c,J$) processes occurring at threshold under the $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV condition. Employing next-to-leading-order perturbation theory in $\alpha_s$, we numerically determine the associated cross sections. Furthermore, we analyze how $v^{(4)}$ influences these angular distributions and present an examination of theoretical uncertainties concerning the angular-dependent parts of the hadronic matrix elements.

This research investigates how everyday Signal users grasp end-to-end encryption and PINs. We conducted 16 in-depth interviews with enthusiastic yet casual users to assess their understanding and usage of these features. Our findings indicate that most participants misunderstood end-to-end encryption, viewing it as a server-side measure affecting message delay rather than a client-side mechanism. Regarding PINs, some believed they protected data at rest on devices, while others thought they secured messages in transit. We achieved these insights by analyzing statements from five conceptual models: Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, System Use Model, Protection Motivation Theory, Theory of Reasoned Action, Theory of Planned Behavior, and others. We believe these results will help encryption software developers design more effective user interfaces and communication strategies.

The general coordinate descent (GCD) algorithm is a widely utilized numerical method for non-convex optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that this new algorithm outperforms the original in both efficiency and convergence speed.

To study the topological flexibility of arithmetic groups, we introduce the concepts of $L^2$-characteristic cycles, $L^2$-volume, and $L^2$-coherence for CW complexes carrying a charm-free action of such a group. The authors demonstrate that for a charm-free arithmetic group acting on a CW complex with finite cohomological dimension, this $L^2$-characteristic is necessarily coherent. Furthermore, we establish rigidity results for these groups by defining $L^2$-Euler characteristics; under specific conditions, changes in the ordinary Euler characteristic force $L^2$-isomorphisms between cohomology modules, which in turn prohibits any topological bending of the underlying space. As a consequence, we derive: the charm of a virtual cohomological finite arithmetic group is either zero or infinite; if the group possesses a charm cycle, it admits no free action on any contractible complex. Additionally, we note the following: the group $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathcal{O}_D)$ (where $D$ is a number field and $\mathcal{O}_D$ its ring of integers) has zero charm whenever the unit rank exceeds 1.

Most work on object pose estimation relies on training data from known classes and suffers the class imbalance issue inherent to retraining models when encountering new categories. This paper introduces a new zero-shot class-level pose estimation approach that addresses this challenge. First, we develop a new representation for object pose using the interaction between 2D and 3d bounding boxes. Second, we train a class-aware model that estimates this representation from images. Third, we develop a linear class-level projection model to generalize the representation to unknown classes. This system estimates the pose for novel classes and generates corresponding 3d bounding boxes from a single image. Predicting traffic flow is a critical component of intelligent transportation systems. While numerous deep learning approaches have been developed, they typically focus on predicting flow for individual road sections, which is inefficient when dealing with extensive networks. This paper introduces a flow estimation technique that leverages temporal and spatial similarities to handle sparse data, allowing for the generation of city-wide forecasts using only measurements from a small subset of sensors. By identifying feature points through self-similarities in time and space, the model learns flow features that can be applied to a weighted similarity approach. This strategy facilitates the prediction of flow across an entire network, shifting the problem from solving traffic equations for every link to estimating just a limited number of features. Experiments indicate that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in predicting flow patterns and exhibits robustness against noisy data.

This paper introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders designed for structure learning with intervention and counterfactual queries. While existing methods typically focus on recovering the causal structure of conStructure, or the global topology of a given set of causal mechanisms, our method goes a step further by enabling the inference of causal mechanisms themselves from data. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets, we demonstrate that VACA successfully learns these structures with high accuracy. Additionally, the framework supports learning with noisy or incomplete data, as well as performing interventional and counterfactual inference based on the recovered models.

In recent years, the rapid evolution of machine learning has catalyzed a paradigm shift within photonics, enabling machine-optimized photonic devices that surpass the capabilities of conventional optimization and ad-hoc designs. This progress has been instrumental in solving complex inverse problems to generate innovative concepts in end-to-end training, machine-controlled quantum photonics, and machine-assisted device fabrication. In this review, we concentrate on the domain of metaphotonics—encompassing metasurfaces, metaatoms, and other metamaterials—as a critical intersection where machine intelligence converges with metaphotonic technology. We highlight how designing machine-learning-augmented metamaterials enables unprecedented control over light-matter interactions, unlocking novel capabilities for both fundamental research and technological advancement.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset comprising 2,000 motion pictures from the top 100 film studios (2000–2020), featuring pre-release attributes such as genre, cast, crew, and production tags. We examine how these pre-release indicators influence box office revenue, employing both supervised and unsupervised learning methodologies. Our findings indicate that while cast talent exerts a significant impact on gross income—often overshadowing other variables—analytical tools derived from the dataset offer actionable insights for industry stakeholders regarding strategic decision-making under uncertainty.

This study demonstrates that the collective dynamics of power systems can be enhanced through frequency regulation, utilizing the network's electrical resonance. To establish this framework, we incorporate auxiliary springs into a classical model of coupled oscillator dynamics. Through linear stability analysis, we identify how control springs allow regulators to harness the network's resonant frequency to maintain voltage stability even within highly synchronous regimes. Furthermore, we establish that optimal performance is achieved when regulatory forces are tuned to synchronize with voltage collapse bifurcation points.

This paper introduces a strategy to bolster large-scale cyber-physical systems of networks by integrating intelligent components into existing networks. We present an initial framework for assessing how artificial intelligence can augment network performance within a "smartified" context, focusing on AI technologies that can be embedded into network infrastructure. Initially, we will examine machine learning and deep learning for in situ applications, followed by an analysis of AI-driven tools for enhancing network security and management. Furthermore, an illustrative scenario involving a significant cyber-physical system will be provided to demonstrate the advantages of integrating intelligent intelligence. Ultimately, this work aims to establish a foundational framework for investigating how AI can strengthen cyber-physical systems viewed as networks of networks.

This study introduces MAPPIES, a Monte-Carlo code designed to simulate synchrotron radiation from partially polarized light interacting with a specific electron distribution. The utility of this tool is demonstrated by analyzing blazar spectra, specifically addressing the origin of the UV and soft X-ray excesses observed in their spectral energy distributions. The analysis relies on a simplified model where the soft X-ray surplus arises from inverse-Compton (IC) scattering of external polarized radiation fields, such as broad-line region photons and jets, rather than synchrotron emission. The simulation compares spectral predictions generated by including external radiation against those from synchrotron alone, using randomly selected relativistic electron distributions to identify optimal fits for spectral energy distributions. The findings indicate that theoretical models aligning with blazar spectra are achievable by applying these multi-component scenarios.

This study presents methods for computing the slope and curvature on complex topographies using locally fitted circular arcs derived from height-height data along multiple data lines. Data from these lines, which are spaced at regular intervals, is used to determine the average height and radius of curvature. A key component involves a procedure for calculating sector areas of circular arcs to derive normalized slope and curvature metrics. These analytical techniques have been implemented in the open-source Python package `geotools` (https://github.com/benno-stolz/geotools).

We introduce a digital approach to identify local invariants for the classification of three-qubit entanglement. As the primary output of this method is the measurement of the three-qubit entanglement measure, we demonstrate its efficacy using the method's primary result on classifying three- and four-part quantum states. By presenting the classification of N-part quantum states, we show its utility in distinguishing different types of multipartite entanglement. The primary advantage of this approach is its ease of implementation in current and near-future experimental settings.

Baryon creation is a fundamental process in the early universe and high-energy particle collisions. We present a novel theoretical framework based on the quantized breakup of helical superfluid filaments to explain baryon formation. In this model, a quantized fragmentation event produces a burst of energy and entropy alongside specific baryonic states. We demonstrate that the resulting flow of superfluid filaments aligns with the baryon-to-photon ratio derived from cosmic microwave background radiation and particle entropy. Furthermore, filament unraveling and reconnection events generate magnetic fields, while the quantized breakdown of helical structures and magnetic recombination processes account for observed dynamo effects. This filament-based theory offers a comprehensive explanation for baryon generation, the early universe's magnetic field origins, and their associated dynamics.

The Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) has been continuously monitoring travel times between travel-time pairs with east-west and north-south orientations since 2010. This study investigates whether flows parallel to the solar equator can be detected using these HMI data. We developed a novel algorithm to measure travel times around active regions, utilizing the ratio of cross-correlation coefficients. Applying this method to HMI data from 2015 to 2017, we found that a significant fraction of measurements showing east-west periodic travel time variations align with movements parallel to the equator, traveling eastward at approximately 100 m s$^{-1}$, consistent with supergranulation. In contrast, north-south measurements reveal no significant periodic variations, indicating anisotropic sensitivity in the travel-time data. Analysis of the observed travel-time variations further suggests that the periodic signals detected in the north-south data are minor compared to those in east-west data.

We introduce a new approach for compressing light field data that leverages a novel model integrating both disparity and visual quality. This proposed Light Field Knowledge-based Unify Model (LLFUM) addresses the inadequacies of existing methods by addressing two critical gaps: the disparity between traditional distortion metrics and human visual systems, and the lack of interaction between disparity and visual quality in current coding strategies. To resolve the visual-quality-versus-distortion mismatch, our framework introduces VQNet, an unifying architecture that accepts disparity as input to adaptively predict visual quality. Furthermore, we employ a VPBAM (Virtual Plane-based Attention Model) to guide compression efforts by pinpointing key regions on virtual planes. These regions are then transmitted via a hybrid coding scheme of context-adaptive binary arithmetic hybrid ( CABAC ) and entropy ( E ) . Experimental results confirm that the framework achieves superior visual fidelity and outperforms current state-of-the-art light field compression techniques.

This study investigates the integration of interactive and non-auto-complet (non-inter) frameworks within vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval (CIL). While recent advancements have focused on the non-inter approach, the inter framework offers distinct advantages by incorporating the entire user query to enhance search precision. We present a unified architecture that leverages both paradigms, allowing the inter component to refine semantic similarity using the full query text and the non-inter component to boost performance through explicit interaction features. Empirical evaluations across multiple cross-lingual benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed unified model attains a substantial improvement of +0.023 in Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and +0.003 in normalized discounted recall (NDCG@1000) when compared to the strongest existing inter-active CIL models.

Small-area estimation (SAE) models are widely employed to produce reliable estimates for regions with limited data availability. However, in many low- and middle-income countries, a critical hurdle remains the lack of granular spatial data at the target Small Area level. Consequently, practitioners often rely on spatial surrogates, such as national or regional census figures, to define spatial structures. This study evaluates the performance of SAE models under these constraints, focusing on two specific scenarios: first, when a national-level survey provides population data that aligns closely with area-specific estimates; and second, when population figures are entirely absent, necessitating the use of spatial survey data with differing total counts (or totals) at the regional scale. A case study utilizing 2010/2011 data from the Malawi National Nutrition Survey, which examined stunting prevalence across its 58 districts, illustrates these scenarios. The analysis compares results from models utilizing direct population figures (Scenario 1) versus those using regional census totals as spatial surrogates (Scenario 2). The findings indicate that while estimated trends and patterns remain consistent across both approaches, discrepancies in prediction accuracy and bias do occur when population figures are unavailable. These results underscore the critical importance of securing high-quality local population data for generating unbiased small-area estimates. The paper concludes by outlining practical recommendations for both exploratory data analysis and model specification to ensure robustness when exact population data is inaccessible.

This paper introduces a continuous-variable methodology for calculating optimal coefficients in quantum waging problems, addressing both the single-asset and multi-asset scenarios. By framing the objective as maximizing the minimum post-bet q-state von Neumann entropy, the solution leverages a recent result from the quantum data processing inequality. The study provides a closed-form expression for the solution to the single-asset case and establishes a bound in the context of multi-asset investments.

The formation of planets relies on disk creation, yet the specific mechanisms governing disk formation remain unclear. While disks are believed to emerge from the collapse of pre-stellar cores, the process is complicated by non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), which can alter angular momentum evolution and mass accretion rates. This study utilizes 2D and 3D magnetized collapse simulations to determine the conditions required for planet-forming disks. We find that in non-ideal MHD scenarios, the accretion rate is set by the initial specific angular momentum of the core, which is primarily influenced by turbulence. This specific accretion rate aligns with values derived from observed protostellar cores. Additionally, the mass of the resulting disk is determined by the initial rotation rate of the pre-stellar core, provided this rotation does not exceed a critical threshold. This critical limit varies based on the magnetic Prandtl number and the orientation of the magnetic field relative to the disk plane. Consequently, disk mass is highly sensitive to these parameters, particularly when turbulence is low. Ultimately, the majority of collapsing cores are expected to produce planet-forming disks, though the specific disk properties depend on the core's angular momentum evolution.

This work addresses the challenge of forecasting temporal series across multiple time dimensions, such as individual days within a week, utilizing deep learning techniques. The proposed approach leverages a hierarchical recurrent neural network (HRNN) architecture, which employs Bayesian variational inference to automatically determine sparse solutions. By learning sparse representations, the model enhances interpretability and generalization. The method was evaluated on two financial datasets—multi-period S&P 500 data and short-term earnings per share (EPS) forecasting using the COMPUSTAT database. Experimental results indicate that the proposed HRNN architecture achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning approach that trains distributed datasets across multiple devices while keeping the data local. The central server coordinates this process by exchanging only model updates with the participating clients. A persistent challenge in FL is ensuring fair model performance across all data sources. This issue is particularly acute when datasets are heterogeneous—varying in size, domain, or quality—leading to significant performance disparities among clients. To illustrate these inequities, we introduce a method for quantifying the fairness of FL models that incorporates privacy protections. By leveraging the framework of $\epsilon$-Differential Privacy, we establish rigorous privacy guarantees for both the server and individual participants during the learning process. Our approach ensures that both entities can recover the heterogeneous equity parameters with high probability, effectively allowing them to infer the underlying fairness characteristics of the dataset. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the number of communication rounds required for this estimation, demonstrating that both the server and clients can determine the equity parameters with high confidence using significantly fewer iterations than the total number of required for model convergence.

We introduce a supersymmetric minimal $U(1)_X$ model featuring a $Z_2$-parity and an abelian gauge symmetry, with the $Z_2$-odd sector including three right-handed Majorana neutrinos. This framework accommodates both a $Z_2$-even Higgs triplet and $Z_2$-odd doublets, which are essential for simultaneously achieving seesaw neutrino masses, generating dark matter, and facilitating the baryon asymmetry of the universe. We demonstrate that the theory remains consistent with current experimental data across the entire parameter space and show that $Z_1$-conservation is a viable candidate for dark matter, with its relic density established through the process of thermal freeze-out. We also analyze the model's phenomenology, showing that the $Z_2$-even Higgs doublet and singlet can be distinguished via the LHC, while the $Z_2$-odd right-handed neutrinos can be identified at the LHC or the future high-luminosity LHC (HL-LHC).

This study presents a novel unsupervised learning-based method for optimizing the throughput of Internet Reflecting Surface (IRS)-supported wireless charging networks (WCNs) that may experience communication disruptions. The primary objective is to maximize system throughput by jointly optimizing the IRS's phase shift configuration and scheduling the scheduling of wireless charging vehicles (WCVs) responsible for battery replenishment. To address this, the paper introduces a Deep Clustering (DC) algorithm that derives an optimal solution by identifying a balanced clustering solution between WRCs and active IRS elements and the WCVs' parking spots for each charging opportunity. Simulation results indicate that the proposed DC strategy significantly boosts network throughput compared to several existing schemes.

We introduce a learning-based approach to control that integrates side information to enhance the efficiency of training non-linear controllers for dynamic systems. Our method uses this supplementary information to shape a control policy, enabling the rapid acquisition of stable gaits within a simplified physical simulator. We demonstrate a side information-based controller capable of mastering multiple complex behaviors—such as running, flying, and swimming—using only a limited number of simulation trials. Our results indicate that this approach achieves superior performance compared to standard learning-based techniques, even when trained on real hardware.

We establish the Ward identities within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory corresponding to the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. These identities are derived from translation, dilatation, and the three generators of $SL_3$. The proof utilizes the associated Feigin-Frenkel-Flato-Zagier representation of the $SL_3$ Lie group acting on the three-variable vertex operator algebra module. Specifically, we demonstrate that the four-point correlation functions of the primary fields obey the standard conformal Ward identities. Furthermore, we establish the explicit link between the higher-rank Feigin-Frenkel-Flato-Zagier representations and the higher-genel Miura transformations. This framework enables us to represent the three-variable vertex operator algebra module as a direct integral of tensor products involving the free-field realization and universal Verma modules.

Graphs are ubiquitous in real-world scenarios, representing diverse entities like people, genes, and cells alongside their intricate connections. Knowledge graphs (KGs) have become a specific type of graph designed to facilitate machine learning on structured information. While recent advancements in combinatorial optimization and Bayesian methods have improvedKGs, deep learning approaches for completing them remain underdeveloped. This paper introduces a novel deep learning framework called Relation GAN (RGAN), an extension of the original Goal-conditioned Generative Adversarial Network (GCGAN) model. RGAN is specifically tailored for knowledge graph learning by generating graphs conditioned on a goal triple consisting of head entity, relation, and tail entity. The primary objective is enhancing the generation performance through two key strategies: (1) incorporating cycle-consistency constraints to improve the quality of generated graph structures, and (2) employing natural language model (NLM)-based goals to address the alignment problem inherent in GCGANs. This approach ensures that generated tail entities are semantically coherent with their corresponding head entity and relation. Furthermore, the paper outlines a new model architecture, Triplet GAN (TrGAN), which further refines performance by extending cycle-consistency constraints to handle all three components of a goal triple. Comprehensive experiments on benchmark KG completion datasets demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art deep learning and traditional non-deep learning models.

This paper introduces a novel Quantum Key Distribution (KPD) protocol relying on a phase-independent coherent state dual-field structure. In this framework, a phase-encoded particle and an amplitude-gage particle constitute the two distinct fields transmitted through an optical fiber channel; notably, the amplitude-gage particle functions without requiring phase stabilization. Security analysis demonstrates that although the phase-encoded particle remains vulnerable to phase-shift attacks, the amplitude-gage particle effectively counters these threats through the influence of quantum non-locality. This design significantly reduces implementation complexity and enhances practicality for real-world quantum communication.

This paper focuses on the Toeplitz algebras formed by Hilbert space projectors on both the Dirichlet and Bergman spaces defined on the unit disk. The analysis reveals that the quasicontinuous functions—specifically those appearing in the Brownian spectrum—serve as the spectrum for the maximal quotient of these algebras. Additionally, the study re-examines the spectrum of Toeplitz operators with Hilbert space symbols on both the Dirichlet and Bergman spaces, and the results are complemented by examples that illustrate how this spectral behavior can defy intuitive expectations.

Current lexical object detection (LexOBJ) methods typically rely on static, fixed object categories such as cars, pedestrians, and bicycles. This limitation stems from the high annotation costs associated with obtaining instance-level bounding box labels, particularly when dealing with open lexicons containing thousands of object classes. To address this, we present a novel approach that infers bounding box annotations directly from image-level labels, thereby eliminating the need for instance-level data. By leveraging large-scale datasets like COCO-Open-X and AIyL to train our model, we demonstrate that it achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art instance-detection systems, even in scenarios constrained by limited instance data.

Transformer models have become a cornerstone in advancing artificial intelligence, particularly within natural language processing (NLP). Despite their recent surge in popularity for audio and visual tasks, a comprehensive survey specifically addressing vision transformer models remains scarce. This paper presents a thorough review of vision transformer architectures, analyzing both current state-of-the-art research and key future research avenues. By critically examining these findings, we aim to support future scholars in accelerating progress across various application domains.

This study addresses the challenge of forecasting total mortality rates utilizing a time-varying factor Shrinkage model. The proposed approach is compared against a conventional benchmark employing time-invariant factor loadings, which incorporates a penalty of logarithmic loss on complex models to enhance predictive accuracy. The results demonstrate that allowing factor loadings to fluctuate over time significantly improves performance in both in-sample and out-of-sample evaluations. This methodology is applied to forecast the total mortality rates for Switzerland, Germany, France, Great Britain, and the EU.

The research also introduces a Bayesian dynamic factor model for predicting future total mortality rates. Neural architecture search (NAS) has become a vital tool for automating neural network architecture design. Despite this, NAS algorithms often struggle to identify superior architectures because sub-searches can interfere with one another. This paper investigates interference in multi-objective NAS frameworks, a common approach for Jointly optimizing task-specific and task-objective-oriented architectures. We discovered that sub-searches can negatively impact one another in two specific ways: through interference induced by shared data and through interference arising from architecture sharing. To address these challenges, we developed a novel strategy to mitigate interference between searches, resulting in improved task-specific and task-objective-oriented architecture performance. Furthermore, we enhance current architecture sharing mechanisms by introducing a compatibility assessment that further inhibits interference. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm and architecture search strategies substantially outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in both task-specific and task-objective-oriented applications across various benchmarks, yielding improved performance metrics for both objectives.

This paper introduces a novel concept of attribute-based time series, where time series data is complemented by auxiliary data that may vary in structure and type. We propose a comprehensive framework for attribute-based time series consisting of four core components: attribute-based forecasting, attribute-based time series examination, attribute-based decomposition, and attribute-based classification. Additionally, we present the R package `t ime s a t t` to provide functional implementations of this framework.

We present a cohomological criterion determining when the boundary of a two-dimensional geodesically complete CAT(0) spacetime admits a free abelian cover. This criterion serves as a revision of the third author's prior work, which established a homological condition for the same property regarding geodesically complete graphs with CAT(0) surface covers.

Over the last decade, machine translation (MT) has advanced significantly, leading to a growing demand for the assessment of its output. While current quality evaluation methods typically rely on comparing system-generated translations against expert translations or targeting them for human review, our work introduces a novel approach to assess MT output from a statistical perspective. By adopting a Bayesian framework, we estimate the probability that a translation is correct, utilizing the alignment statistics between well-aligned sentences and those containing errors. This method requires only the target systems' translations and does not involve human translators. Consequently, it establishes a new, objective upper limit on machine translation quality. Furthermore, the model enables fair comparison across different systems and provides each translation with a specific reliability score.

Scattering systems, such as disordered media and photonic nanostructures, can absorb substantial energy from incoming waves. When absorption occurs within the system's local mode spectrum, the dominant energy absorption pathways correspond to specific channels known as eigenchannels. Although these have been the subject of extensive study in simpler contexts, their behavior remains poorly understood for systems characterized by spatially varying parameters. This work introduces two general theorems to clarify energy absorption eigenchannels in scattering systems with spatially non-uniform characteristics. Furthermore, the authors present an approximate formula for estimating the number of these eigenchannels that approach unit probability of occurrence.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, yet their key advantages remain unclear. This study investigates the luster of CNNs by contrasting them with winning lottery tickets within fully linked networks (FLNs). Specifically, it explores two fundamental distinctions: first, whether CNNs enable more efficient feature extraction by sifting irrelevant information from images through localized filters, and second, whether they offer a more energy-efficient learning trajectory compared to FLNs. Our findings indicate that CNNs do not possess an inherent edge over FLNs in feature selection efficiency. Furthermore, contrary to expectations, CNNs exhibit less efficient learning dynamics than FLNs. Consequently, the superior performance of CNNs cannot be attributed to inherent structural superiority; rather, it stems from the ability to identify and train these networks more effectively.

The demand for lottery tickets is driven by how people anticipate lotto outcomes, which are inherently uncertain and vary based on past results and historical sales. This paper introduces a new model that accounts for these demand dynamics to determine the optimal timing for both outcome realization (when to sell) and purchase (when to consume). Unlike traditional approaches, the proposed framework treats the lotto ticket's value as the maximum of the purchase price and the sale price, with the sale value being an adaptively chosen function of historical result and sales history. This innovative, adaptive selling mechanism is shown to yield higher expected profits for the seller and, consequently, greater utility for the purchaser compared to standard systems, while also allowing the seller to maintain higher expected profits even when offering lower prices.

We present the computation of the $(\phi^Q)^2\phi$ vertex at six loops for the $O(N)$ symmetric model, where the coupling $Q$ takes the specific value of $5/2$. This calculation is performed using the method of background field techniques at that order. When the parameter $N$ is taken to the large limit, this result allows us to determine the anomalous (or total) dimension of the $\phi^Q$ operator at six-loop precision within the non-trivial fixed point of the $N \to \infty$ $O(N)$ model. We also provide numerical estimates for the case $N=2$ and the theoretical large-$N$ limit. Additionally, we calculate the total self-energy up to five-loop order in the same large-$N$ framework. By combining these results with the known interaction vertex, we derive the total exponent for the operator $\phi^2$ to six-loop order (or $\phi^Q$ to six-loop order) within the $N \to \infty$ limit.

Valley degrees of freedom in two-dimensional materials are exceptionally sensitive to perturbations, particularly electronic-phonon interactions, which can disrupt valley stability. In this study, we investigate valley relaxation dynamics in monolayer tungsten trioxide (1T-WO3) and phosphorene, focusing on the influence of these interactions. The analysis reveals that phonon scattering rates in 1T-WT-WO3 and phosphorene are governed by two unique mechanisms: electron-mediated phonon deformation and intravalley scattering. The former occurs when an electron absorbs or emits a phonon while switching valleys, whereas the latter involves the conversion between spin states. We demonstrate that these pathways can act either cooperatively or antagonistically to relax valleys, depending on the specific energy mismatch between valleys and the mode of the electron-phonon coupling employed. Consequently, these findings underscore the necessity of accounting for both phonon deformation and scattering channels when analyzing valley relaxation in semiconducting 1T-WT-WO3 and phosphorene.

The Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge at NeurIPS 2022 evaluated methods designed to create generalization capabilities for new, unseen, and unlabeled target domains using a multi-task framework. To address this, our approach synthesizes multiple solutions derived from leading state-of-the-art methods and re-trains the models to effectively handle target domain data. Experiments conducted on this configuration achieved a performance gain of 1.5% over the second-best entry and secured the #1 rank among all participants.

M dimensional spherical data is frequently observed in diverse fields, including natural language processing, computer vision, and physics. However, many machine learning techniques rely on Euclidean data and require representation learning to adapt to spherical formats. We introduce a novel version of the t-SNE algorithm specifically for spherical data, termed Spherical Manifold Neighboring Embedding (SNE). Our method preserves the core philosophy of t-SNE but replaces all distance calculations with those suitable for spherical contexts. Additionally, we present two distance metrics for spheres: one based on Fréchet Inclusion Distance and another proposed by our authors. Experimental results using synthetic datasets and the Google Image Spheres benchmark confirm that this approach significantly outperforms existing spherical representation methods.

This study examines zero-temperature pasing of the Fermi polaron across dimensions of two and three space using the Diagram Monte Carlo (DMC) method. By employing DMC, we compute closed Green functions for closed diagrams representing specific interaction processes. Combining these with closed and open diagram contributions allows for the calculation of the polaron's self-energy, which is then used to determine the renormalized mass and binding energy. Our results for the fermi polaron in two dimensions are compared against Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, demonstrating strong qualitative and quantitative agreement. Furthermore, we analyze how Green functions, self-energy, the renormalized mass, and binding energy vary with the interaction strength.

We introduce a hybrid analog-digital approach to (i) benchmark the efficiency of digital fermion mappings and (ii) mitigate non-Markovian noise effects in quantum simulations. By combining unitary auxiliary fields with fermionic density matrix quantum tomography, this method optimizes quantum circuits for representing ground states while utilizing external fields to model dynamic evolution. The density matrix technique allows for precise ground state estimation, whereas the unitary auxiliary field approach facilitates efficient time evolution of the Hamiltonian. Applied to the Hubbard model, numerical results demonstrate that incorporating this hybrid strategy significantly reduces the number of quantum gates and renders the simulation robust against environmental noise.

This work investigates properties of polynomial sequences derived from properties of graphs colored with $k$ colors. We specifically focus on the all-subtree series of these colored graphs. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between the all-subtree series and the all-subtopology series, establishing a formula to calculate the coefficient of the polynomial of degree $r$ within the degree $(r+1)$ polynomial. The analysis also details the differential equation satisfied by the all-subtree series for path graphs. Furthermore, the sequence itself exhibits specific regularity patterns across varying degrees. The findings include the asymptotic expansion for the polynomials of all-path trees and a characterization of complex symmetry found within the series for stars. Finally, the study establishes links between the colored all-subtree series of stars and Bessel functions, as well as the series for stars minus their centers and the modified Bessel functions.

Conventional project management frameworks like PRINCE2 and PMBOK are process-heavy and often fail to address the evolving needs of modern software development, leading many organizations to adopt Agile methodologies. Within the software industry, Scrum is the most prevalent of these, yet its reliance on face-to-face interactions—such as daily stand-ups and sprint reviews—faces challenges as remote telecommuting becomes increasingly popular. This paper critically examines how a shift to telecommuting impacts Scrum project performance, exploring the trade-offs between the flexibility of remote work and the structural requirements of Agile. Through two studies—first analyzing 100 telecommuting Scrum projects and second interviewing 120 team members and managers—we find that while efficiency and morale improve and job satisfaction remains stable, overall project success declines. These findings offer practical guidance for both practitioners and leaders considering remote work in an Agile context.

The authors introduce the concept of a Gu-Wu value for matrix forms and investigate the associated Gu-Wu values in two specific cases: $4 \times 4$ and truncated choose arrowhead matrices. By deriving the relevant Gau-Wu values, the authors also present the Gaussian elimination process. The results include the G-W values for a $4 \times 4$ matrix, where the diagonal elements are $a_{11}=a_{22}=a_{33}=a_{44}=1$ and off-diagonal entries are $a_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$. Additionally, the results cover a truncated choose arrowhead matrix with $a_{11}=1$ and $a_{ij}=1$ elsewhere, noting that $a_{ij}=0$ when $i,j \geq 2$ and $i \neq j$. The total number of operations (flops) for Gauss elimination in a general $n \times n$ matrix is approximately $n^3/3$.

This study examines the elliptic flow, $v_2$, of beauty-hadron decay products within central Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. Utilizing data from the ALICE experiment at the LHC, we analyzed centralities ranging from 0–60\% across transverse momentum ($p_\mathrm{T}$) intervals of 0.5 to 6.0 GeV/$c$. Our analysis contrasts the $K^0_\mathrm{S}$-s and $\pi^\pm$ $v_2$ distributions, which are interpreted as originating from charm and light-flavour quarks respectively, against the $B^0$ and $B^\mp$ (interpreted as $\pi^{\mp}$ in some contexts but here specifically $B^0$ and $B^\mp$ in the text) $v_2$ signatures attributed to beauty decays. The findings reveal that the $B^0$ and $B^\mp$ $v_2$ values are notably lower than those of $\pi^{\mp}$ but closely match the $K^0_\mathrm{S}$ $v_2$ over the entire $p_\mathrm{T}$ spectrum. An $S^1$-space $X$ qualifies as a Chromatic $\alpha$-structure (or $\alpha$-structure for short) if it satisfies: (i) $X$ is a finite $S^1$-Torus $S^1 T$-space; (ii) the fixed points of $X$ under the action of the subgroup $\mathbb{Z}_m \subset S^1$ collectively form a union of spheres for every integer $m \geq 2$. This research demonstrates that the reduced Steadfast homology of such structures yields a novel invariant, which is independent of the choice of subgroup $\mathbb{Z}_m \subset S^1$ used to define them. As an illustration of this new invariant's power, we provide a concise proof of the Longotzki conjecture, recently established by Grane and Ye.

This paper investigates the performance gap between optimal and binary power levels in $K$-user interference networks. We demonstrate that even with binary power control, the achievable Extremal GDoF approaches the optimal value with a precision of $\Theta(\frac{1}{\log^2\log N})$. Consequently, the penalty for not utilizing binary power is nearly minimal. However, when comparing against a specific binary strategy, optimal GDoF degrades by $\Theta(\frac{\sqrt{K}}{\log\log N})$ bits relative to that approach. This implies that binary power regulation can yield an advantage of up to $\Theta(\frac{\sqrt{K}}{\log\log N})$ over optimal regulation relative to some optimal point. This result highlights the importance of binary power strategies in scenarios where the number of users is large.

Auditing is a meticulous process of evaluating the governance, administration, and control systems of an organization, which necessitates the application of data mining and machine learning to analyze vast datasets. This study introduces a mining approach that incorporates the unique characteristics of auditing data, which are often imbalanced, contain significant noise, and exist in varying levels of abstraction. The core of this methodology relies on two innovations: first, the use of formal concept analysis (FCA) to construct a hierarchical classification scheme, and second, the application of Dempster-Shafer theory to perform a reliable Bayesian classification. The proposed system was piloted within an external audit context, and the resulting evidence suggests it is a promising new approach for auditing applications.

This work presents sample complexity bounds for the Strauss point process, assuming the existence of an exact full conditional distribution. The primary contribution is a novel exact sampling algorithm for Strauss configurations within a general linear graph $L$, which builds upon the coupling of two point processes—a Poisson distribution with intensity $\mu/2$ and the configuration $\Xi_L$ of an exact realization of the Strauss process restricted to $L$—each selected with probability $1/2$. The paper situates the existing algorithms by M\"uller (2000) and Bandyopadhyay and Szabó (2015) as specific implementations of this coupling approach. Finally, the study derives sampling bounds for the complete Strauss process by applying the primary algorithm sequentially across an expanding sequence of finite sub-regions that collectively cover the space.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), grounded in string theory, offers valuable insights into quantum gravity effects. This study examines a GUP-informed particle model, applying Galilean transformations followed by Lorentz transformations to its coordinates and momenta. We demonstrate that the translated dynamics remain consistent with Hagen's theorem, even though the specific forms of the Hamiltonian and commutators shift due to the altered structure. Consequently, the deformation of Galilean transformations persists after the Lorentz transformation is applied. Furthermore, the translation generator within the Lorentz group no longer commutes with boost generators, indicating a deformed Poincaré algebra. Finally, the algebraic breakdown of spacetime symmetries is elaborated, and the physical implications of the resulting deformed dynamics are discussed.

We investigate the multi-objective timetabling problem, specifically focusing on the trade-off between minimizing student conflicts and minimizing teacher schedule density. This problem is modeled as a lexicographic optimization with two distinct objectives. To address the first, we employ multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) to generate diverse, high-quality solutions. For managing the second objective, we implement a time- and resource-aware operating system, which is typically used to schedule tasks, within the evolutionary framework. This innovative system enables the concurrent processing of multiple sub-solutions, thereby improving overall computational efficiency. The approach was evaluated using the standard 2017 University of Timișoara dataset, with experimental results demonstrating that the OS-based scheduling component successfully achieves significant performance gains.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, establishing itself as a critical component of the 4G/5G ecosystem. A fundamental challenge for IoT devices is ensuring reliable data transmission, which becomes particularly difficult in large-scale mesh networks where nodes can be geographically dispersed and operating conditions are unpredictable. Firmware updates are essential for enhancing security and functionality in these systems; however, over-the-air (OTA) upgrades often fail in the dynamic and demanding environment of mesh IoT. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of firmware update mechanisms within large-scale mesh topologies. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that current update mechanisms are insufficient for handling the dynamics of real-world mesh networks, thereby failing to meet dependability standards. Consequently, we introduce a new approach designed to facilitate successful firmware upgrades in practical deployments.

Multifractal properties characterize eigenstates in non-interacting disordered systems situated deep within the ergodic regime. This study examines how these signatures of non-multifractality shift toward the non-interacting multfractal many-body localized (MBL) phase as weak interactions are introduced, aiming to determine the transition point for small Fock spaces. Our findings reveal that the Fock-space eigenstate propagator, $e^{-E\Delta t}$, decays exponentially with a non-trivial effective exponent governing time evolution. This exponential term reveals a scaling behavior in the many-body transition. This behavior of the decay rate with the system size and the energy exhibits a non-linear scaling, which shifts towards the interaction-dependent multifractal transition. This study examines the budget-interactive query complexity required to identify $\tau$ hidden items with $\theta$ support within an ordered list of $n$ items, utilizing adaptive queries. A query for index $i$ returns the number of hidden items located at indices $j \geq i$. We demonstrate that identifying $\tau$ hidden items with $\theta$ support necessitates at least $\Omega(\theta \log n + \log \log n + \log \tau)$ queries when the algorithm is restricted to a sample size of $\theta$. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm that identifies these hidden items using exactly $\mathcal{O}(\theta \log n + \log \tau + \log \log n)$ queries, establishing that this complexity is optimal up to constant factors. We also present an exact characterization of the maximum number of hidden items identifiable with $\theta$ queries, which depends linearly on the query budget and asymptotically matches $n$ in the high-budget limit.

Quantum machine learning offers a promising avenue for training models on extensive datasets, but the impact of adversarial attacks on the classification accuracy of these models has not yet been adequately investigated. This thesis addresses this gap by globally assessing the vulnerability of various quantum neural networks to different types of attacks. To achieve this, a novel framework for creating adversarial training instances and disturbances is established. Specifically, three distinct attack strategies are examined: pixel-wise attacks, localized attacks, and attacks that target specific bits within the quantum model. The study confirms that quantum classifiers are susceptible to these threats, demonstrating that their behavior under adversarial pressure closely resembles that of classical neural networks.

The primary objective of this work is to analyze the Steklov spectrum of open bounded subsets within $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are nearly spherical in nature. By establishing an asymptotic approximation for these eigenvalues, we demonstrate the stability of their associated eigenfunctions.

Compliance constitutes a pivotal aspect of contemporary business operations, with compliance checking serving as a core component of that domain. Although inferring business process models from execution logs has been extensively explored, the problem of verifying whether execution traces adhere to a predefined set of rules or constraints remains less addressed. Traditional approaches typically treat full compliance checking as an extension of conformance checking, relying on heavy-weight techniques like token-based model checking that demand substantial modeling effort. This research introduces a lightweight compliance checking approach that examines trace segments against the token flows of the underlying process model without requiring full system mapping. By integrating infix alignments to capture concurrent token flows and postfix alignments to manage prior flows, the proposed infix–postfix weighting ensures accurate verification across all necessary flow types. Unlike model checking, this method avoids dependencies on specific process models, though it still requires access to the source executable model. The proposed tracing technique is evaluated using real-world compliance scenarios and benchmark datasets, with results indicating that it is both more efficient and precise than existing solutions.

Accurate radio signal propagation modeling is essential for the performance analysis and optimization of next-generation communication systems. While analytical models are simple but often lack accuracy, and empirical models are highly precise yet difficult to adapt to new scenarios, this work introduces a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) framework to address these limitations. By leveraging the flexibility of neural networks and the adaptability of empirical approaches, the proposed model utilizes a broad spectrum of environmental data to generate precise predictions. The model's effectiveness was validated using extensive drive test data from real-world deployments, demonstrating significant performance gains over traditional methods.

This work introduces a standardized semantic framework for temporal planning, established through the inaugural International Conference on Temporal Planning (TCP-1) held in 2021. To facilitate research and ensure fair evaluation of planners, these semantics define key concepts such as temporal planning problems, problem instances, and their solutions, while specifying both discrete-time and continuous-time execution models for solvers. The study provides formality proofs for the soundness and completeness of a specific evaluation algorithm within this framework. Consequently, this method is confirmed to yield correct results under the defined semantic semantics and can serve as a authoritative reference for assessing existing and emerging temporal planning solvers.

We investigate a specific class of power network expansion models characterized by convex cost structures, network congestion, and capacities on lines and generators. For a case involving piecewise linear strictly increasing cost curves, we establish a upper bound on the gap between the optimal solution of such an expansion model and its Lagrangian dual. This finding has two significant implications: first, it provides a strong duality guarantee for the Lagrangian dual when gap bounds are sufficiently small, and second, it confirms that these expansion models are highly responsive, meaning their optimal solutions change substantially whenever the optimal costs shift notably. Consequently, these models act as responsive indicators, offering a useful mechanism to efficiently pinpoint critical parameter values that drive cost fluctuations.

This paper examines a Vlasov-Poisson-like system confined to a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, characterized by specific boundary conditions for the distribution function. Such Vlasov frameworks are essential for modeling particle dynamics in particle accelerators, including the recent Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and muon colliders. We demonstrate the existence of global-in-time unique solutions starting from bounded initial conditions that satisfy specific regularity and positivity requirements. Furthermore, we establish that the fields remain uniformly bounded over time, with asymptotic behavior converging to steady states sharing the characteristics of the initial distribution. These findings extend the existing literature, which has primarily addressed such systems in the context of Fusions.

Although numerous research efforts have been dedicated to identifying mentions of entities within text, automatic systems for detecting specific concepts within sentences remain scarce. To address this gap, we introduce the automatic Concept Positioning (CP) task, which involves locating the textual span corresponding to a given concept within a sentence, given its definition. To solve this, we release the initial automatic CP dataset consisting of 123k manually annotated examples across eight diverse domains. Since existing neural models struggle to generalize in this context due to the challenge of aligning ambiguous natural language queries with precise sentence spans, we develop the Strict method for concept detection. Strict employs large pre-trained models equipped with a new data retrieval mechanism that aligns concept definitions with relevant text spans. This approach demonstrates superior performance over both our baseline models and previous state-of-the-art techniques.

Colloidal gels, characterized by a network of entangled and arrested fibers that yield macroscopic mechanical strength, serve as essential building blocks in numerous applications. However, their mechanical properties often lack tunability under specific environmental conditions, limiting their utility. This research demonstrates a method to regulate the viscoelastic behavior of colloidal gels by applying an oscillatory oscillatory field using an ultrasonic resonator. When applied to a gel sample, the resonant device induces transient oscillations lasting several minutes during which the yield stress temporarily decreases, allowing the material to transition from a solid to a liquid state upon the application of minimal shear. Notably, once the ultrasonic vibrations cease and after a specific settling period, the material spontaneously recovers its original viscoelastic characteristics. This work establishes a novel avenue for the temporary, non-invasive, and controllable modification of the viscoelastic properties of gels without the need to disrupt their internal fiber network.

In number theory, the Collatz conjecture is a renowned yet unproven mathematical puzzle. It relies on a straightforward algorithm applied to any positive integer $n$: multiples of three increase to the next power of two by multiplying by two and adding one; otherwise, the number is simply doubled. The conjecture posits that every sequence generated will eventually reach one. Despite the simplicity of this rule, the theory has baffled mathematicians for over eighty years due to its profound complexity and elusive nature. In an attempt to shed light on this mystery, we have explored various statistical methods to analyze the behavior of these sequences and identify any hidden patterns.

Categorizing within the STEM domain is essential for advancing downstream applications such as question-answering and text summarization. Although current state-of-the-art neural network methods achieve high accuracy in this area, they function as "black boxes," offering little insight into the reasoning behind their categorization decisions. To address this lack of interpretability, this study introduces a method that clarifies model predictions by identifying key mathematical entities and the dependencies among them. By revealing these critical mathematical features and their associations, researchers can gain a deeper insight into how models make specific STEM categorization choices.

In the context of a $2n$-player game where participants are paired into two groups of $n$, the objective is to identify the optimal way to assign pairs. Players can only agree on a pairing if the resulting configuration benefits every member compared to rejection. Addressing this challenge, our work introduces a "stable pairing" that ensures each participant finds the assigned arrangement at least as advantageous as proposing to keep it open. To achieve this, the paper presents a "stable proposal" framework, enabling the players to collectively submit a subset of potential matches. This approach offers a more practical and versatile solution than the traditional requirement for a complete stable matching, which necessitates players to reach consensus and agree on a single final outcome. We establish that any proposal mechanism capable of ensuring a supermodular payoff function will also guarantee a stable outcome. Our analysis of player communication reveals that a stable proposal can be successfully identified by a group of $k$ players in $O(n^k)$ time, whereas determining a stable matching for the entire group of $2n$ players demands $O(n^k)$ time.

Generating concise yet comprehensive summaries is a pivotal natural language processing challenge. While numerous summarization models have been proposed, most models are trained using cross-encoders, which inherently operate in a delayed-feedback loop as automated evaluation metrics typically rely on human-annotated references. This reliance on expensive, manual labeling renders automatic metrics impractical for application-specific domains, such as summarizing medical texts, where expert knowledge is scarce. This paper introduces SummScore, a novel, automated metric for summarization quality that employs off-the-shelf cross-encoders to compare a generated summary against a database of diverse reference summaries created by other models. This innovative approach facilitates the large-scale assembly of reference materials and makes the metric fully automatic. Comprehensive experiments conducted on six standard benchmarks demonstrate that SummScore significantly outperforms existing automatic and manual evaluation methods.

We investigate methods for recovering an unknown, real-valued signal from random quadratic observations. This framework encompasses critical problems such as measuring electrical currents via nonlinear inductors and scattering reconstruction in imaging. We introduce a semi-blind iterative algorithm that efficiently and precisely restores signals, which is shown to be a special instance of broader frameworks including iterative thresholding and maximum likelihood estimation. A key advantage of our specific method is its ability to repair anomalous regions in the data, a feature not always achievable by alternative approaches. We establish rigorous convergence bounds for the spectral properties of the estimator in relation to the true underlying signal. Additionally, extensive numerical experiments are provided to demonstrate the method's performance.

Sensor fusion is a critical component of 3D object detection, as it enables multiple sensors to complement each other's weaknesses. However, existing methods are often complex and suboptimal, relying on mismatching strategies such as detecting in one feature space and performing NMS after bounding box expansion, or employing mismatched feature dimensions. In this work, we present BEVFusion, a straightforward yet powerful LiDAR-camera fusion framework that aligns features in the Bird's-Eye-View plane and executes multi-scale detection. Unlike prior complex methods, BEVFusion utilizes simple yet effective fusion mechanisms to generate unified multi-sensor features, which are then processed through a standard multi-scale detector. Our approach significantly lowers implementation complexity while delivering competitive performance across all benchmarks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BEVFusion surpasses state-of-the-art multi-fusion methods in most scenarios, achieving a 0.003 to 1.003 mAP increase on KITTI, and matching or exceeding them on nuScenes. Additionally, our method outperforms single-modality approaches across the KITTI dataset. The project is publicly available at https://github.com/lyu-lyu/BEVFusion.

This work presents a new theoretical framework for incompressible, homogeneous fluid turbulence, incorporating heating and cooling processes. Central to this model is the hypothesis that temperature fluctuations remain turbulent only if heat is removed through dissipation; conversely, they do not exhibit turbulence under adiabatic (no-flow) conditions. We establish the co-spectrality of velocity and thermal turbulence across the inertial regime, which results in a universal expression for the effective heat diffusivity in a fully turbulent state. Additionally, the turbulence of temperature is shown to be confined to the dissipation scale, a phenomenon that helps explain the weak diffusion of heat and momentum observed in all turbulent flows. The utility of the proposed model is validated by its strong alignment with experimental data and numerical simulations.

This study introduces a numerical model to analyze the laser-induced thermal distribution in liquids, aiming to explain the complex diffraction patterns generated by the liquid's lensing effect. While previous investigations have relied on approximations to address specific scenarios, this work employs the time-resolved, one-dimensional heat conduction equation, accounting for laser energy absorption, energy density, and heat flux to generate an accurate simulation of thermal profiles across both the laser interaction duration and subsequent cooling phases. The findings demonstrate that the experimental Self-Diffraction (SD) and Diffraction-Interference (DI) patterns emerge from a progressive shift in the spatial characteristics of the thermal lens; specifically, both the position and the strength of the lens focal points and central region evolve over time due to differing energy absorption rates between the surface-bounded liquid and its bulk.

Design dialogues within the context of software development frequently encompass both human designers and computer systems, often incorporating planning and reasoning to facilitate decision-making. While existing computer-aided design decision support systems rely on mined design dialogues, current datasets suffer from insufficient volume and varied structural definitions, resulting in the development of divergent system architectures. This paper presents "ConDiMiner," a universal miner capable of robustly extracting designs dialogues across multiple datasets despite structural inconsistencies. An evaluation utilizing three established decision support systems against public dataset collections demonstrates that "ConDiMiner" outperforms four existing alternative miners in both absolute performance metrics and robustness.

A primary challenge in data streaming analytics is the growing volume of data generated by numerous sources, which overwhelms traditional database systems. Consequently, specialized systems like TAO and TAO have emerged to address stream processing and real-time querying. However, these systems often lack support for complex analytical capabilities. Consequently, TAO and TAO have been developed to fill this void, enabling flexible data processing and providing effective tools for historical analysis.

A key limitation of these systems is the absence of a unified framework for managing streaming data and historical archives. Consequently, H-STREAM was introduced to serve as a comprehensive solution that effectively handles streaming processing, historical querying, and analytical needs. The system's architecture consists of two primary components: a streaming engine and a relational historical manager. The relational historical manager stores stream data and facilitates query operations, while the streaming engine processes live flows and optimizes storage within the relational historical manager.

A key component of H-STREAM is a new data structure called the "Hybrid Trie" which combines elements of both a Trie and an R-Tree. This data structure is used to organize stream data and facilitate efficient query operations. H-STREAM has been evaluated through a comparison with TAO and Z-Tree, and the results demonstrate that it outperforms these systems in terms of query speed and overall efficiency.

This work investigates the non-resonant production of single top and bottom quark-antiquark pairs ($tbs$ or $tbS$) through $W$-gluon fusion, involving $WS$ exchange in the $t$-channel. We analyze this mechanism within the framework of Heavy Mass Effective Field Theory (HEFT), utilizing a Higgs sector that aligns with the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) structure. We derive the non-resonant graph cross-sections for the MSSEM type-I limit, incorporating $A_f$ and $\tan\beta$ as key variables. Our analysis reveals that, for Type-I MSSEM structures, the top and bottom cross-sections exhibit complementary behaviors with respect to $A_f$ and $\tan\beta$. We also examine the interplay between this non-resonant process and the resonant production of top-bottom pairs via single top or bottom resonance, considering constraints from LHC Run 1 data. Our results demonstrate that, for specific parameter values, the non-resonant component can significantly impact the total cross-section. Furthermore, we evaluate the sensitivity of the extracted top and bottom masses to this non-resonant contribution. We conclude that, in the MSSEM type-I framework, accounting for this non-resonant contribution is essential for precisely determining top and bottom masses.

Knowledge Graphs (KGs) have become increasingly vital in artificial intelligence and semantic web applications. A growing challenge involves transferring such knowledge across different KG components, a problem that relies heavily on machine translation (MT) systems. However, existing MT approaches face significant drawbacks: statistical machine translation (SMT) demands extensive training data and suffers from slow inference, while neural machine translation (NNMT) often generates inaccurate terminology and suffers from high memory consumption. To address these issues, this paper introduces a duplicate mechanism for efficiently managing components within knowledge graphs. This approach enhances NNMT accuracy and decreases its memory footprint without compromising execution speed. Consequently, our method offers a viable solution for performing maintenance tasks on machine translations of edges within semantic knowledge graphs.

The academic community increasingly relies on citation counts to evaluate research impact, yet this metric is often flawed as a sole measure of quality. To address this gap, we introduce VenueInsights, a tool that replaces citation-based metrics with a set of a venue-specific indicators derived from database metadata. These indicators aim to provide a comprehensive overview of a venue's characteristics. Our analysis reveals that most are smooth temporal trends, though they can occasionally exhibit sudden shifts due to significant community events. We validate the utility of these metrics by examining major conferences in machine learning and assessing their effectiveness across diverse venue contexts.

This paper investigates neural network (NN) controllers within the context of stabilizing dynamical systems. It establishes sufficient conditions for the asymptotic stability of such systems, contingent on the verification of specific properties by the NN. Furthermore, the research addresses scenarios involving uncertainties within the NN controller, deriving an explicit upper limit on the magnitude of these system perturbations that guarantees asymptotic stability. To validate these theoretical findings, simulations utilizing a swinging pendulum as the test case are presented.

This study introduces a hierarchical group formulation that effectively manages overlapping structures. Our group assignment function is convex, enabling a single-group-to-single-group assignment for every entity, which subsequently facilitates grouping at all necessary levels. Our innovation lies in using multiple non-convex inter-group potential functions to capture non-linear relationships and overlaps among groups. The equation remains amenable to fully parallelized, fully implicit second-order optimization techniques. Restoring visual data from incomplete observations is a critical challenge in many fields, including medical imaging, remote sensing, and video processing. This paper introduces a new low-rank tensor recovery framework designed to handle streaming video recovery using an adaptive, patch-based monitoring system. The method's effectiveness relies on two key components: a patch monitoring system that dynamically identifies significant regions and directs computational resources accordingly, and a Tensor Splitting Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier (TsALM) framework enhanced with Tensor Splitting (TS). The monitoring system leverages the tensor inductive representation, which is capable of self-supervised learning to adapt resource allocation to areas requiring it most. The Tensor (T) Splitter+Augmented Lagrang multipliers (L) method (T+ALM) algorithm integrates this approach by combining tensor splitting with augmented Lagrangian multipliers to improve convergence speed and efficiency. The method's performance was evaluated against two established techniques: the streaming tensor ring (TR) recovery algorithm and the streaming tensor ring (TR) recovery algorithm with augmented (L) multipliers (TL). The experimental results indicate that the proposed approach achieves superior performance compared to both baseline methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, achieving better results than both baseline methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
