This study employs direct numerical simulations to investigate the spectral properties of inertial wave turbulence within the rotating Navier-Stokes equations. We confirm the presence of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) inertial wave range, demonstrating that its onset is dictated by the anisotropy of energy-containing scales. Unlike previously documented in geophysical fluid dynamics simulations, our findings reveal that the ZK range extends significantly further into the dissipation scale, a behavior attributed to the highly localized nature of energy loss. We also demonstrate the efficacy of the random forcing method in effectively driving inertial wave turbulence.

This work examines the computational complexity of determining the largest independent set in general graphs, focusing on whether well-standardized sublinear-time greedy algorithms can efficiently standardize these instances. Specifically, the authors demonstrate that if any well-standardized sublinear-time algorithm existed for generating maximum-weight autonomous sets in the domain of subcubic, chordless, subgraph-minimal non-perfect graphs, it could be leveraged to design a comparable algorithm for the maximum independent problem within the class of subcubic minimal non-bipartite graphs. Since the existence of the latter is currently unknown, the findings establish significant domain restrictions on the feasibility of efficient iterative graph standardization procedures.

The emergence of graphene has generated significant interest in its potential to be integrated into future electronic components. While standard Graphene exhibits a zero bandgap, tailored methods can induce non-zero bandgaps in this material. This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of a gated single-layer graphene model featuring a non-zero bandgap. We demonstrate that the free energy of this non-equilibrium configuration can be split into a sum representing the respective contributions of band engineering and external biasing. Additionally, we analyze the steady-state heat flow within a single graphene layer connected to heat reservoirs and regulated by a voltage gate. Our findings indicate that the device functions as a heat engine, capable of delivering electrical power while simultaneously expelling waste heat through one of its interfaces. Furthermore, we illustrate how adjusting both the bandgap and gate voltage enables control over the device's operational mode, allowing it to serve either as an energy generator producing electricity or a thermoelectric cooler.

We report the detection of low-frequency radio emissions from the binary system CR Dra, featuring flaring M-dwarfs, utilizing the UTR-2 antenna. The system's radio output is dominated by the electron-cyclotron maser mechanism, driven primarily by flares on the more magnetized of the two stars. The analysis reveals that the mean daily flux density averages approximately 0.04 mJy, with sporadic bursts reaching up to 0.2 mJy. Furthermore, the flare-associated radio activity is observed to vary significantly over a cycle extending of several months.

Human virtual avatars are increasingly prevalent in online social networks, video conferencing, and live streaming platforms. Although many existing systems utilize 3D mesh models to render these avatars, they typically fail to accurately represent real human body movements. ANR (Articulated Neural Rendering) addresses this shortcoming by employing a neural renderer to produce high-fidelity photorealistic images from a new architecture that models a 3D human skeleton and its connected organs as a set of deformed cylinders. Each cylinder is trained on a human-specific dataset using differentiable simulation to learn how they interact and control the organs attached to them. The system employs a differentiable renderer to end-to-end-optimize the 3D neural representations based on video input, allowing dynamic tracking of human deformation. Experiments on a novel motion capture database featuring a digital avatar confirm that this method precisely follows articulated movements while producing realistic imagery. The code and models can be accessed at https://cvml.ml/ANR/.

The proliferation of image enhancement tools and deepfake technologies has intensified scrutiny on how humans and AI systems evaluate visual evidence. Leveraging a curated collection of manipulated news photographs, this study examines the perceptual biases of both human evaluators and machine learning models, specifically focusing on the impact of alteration intensity. Through experiments involving 722 human participants and 16,800 automated predictions, researchers discovered conflicting trends: as image modification becomes more severe, humans actually decrease their likelihood of identifying specific events, likely due to the changes obscuring recognizable details. Conversely, AI models maintain or even increase their predictive confidence with intensified alterations, highlighting fundamental discrepancies in how humans and machines interpret visual fidelity against potential manipulation.

We root our analysis in Edward Witten's foundational work, which establishes a correspondence between three-dimensional Chern-Simons theory and two-dimensional conformal field theory via boundary interactions on three-manifolds with boundaries. We performed cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations on frustrated spin-1/2 antiferromagnets featuring a triangular unit cell with coupled trimers, specifically analyzing the model applicable to the $\rm CrI_3$ monolayer. Our findings demonstrate that this system exhibits 1D long-range order superimposed on the 2D lattice, characterized by the alignment of trimer spins into columns. Remarkably, orientational order within the trimers occurs at significantly higher temperatures than the onset of trimer alignment, a behavior that aligns with mean-field theory predictions. Furthermore, temperature-dependent results from these clusters match those from quantum Monte Carlo methods applied to a 1D trimer-column subsystem, confirming the validity of this approach for probing the physical properties of $\rm CrI_3$.

Although Language Models (LMs) have achieved remarkable success in natural language processing (NLP), they are currently applied to a zero-shot setting involving task-prompt pairs, where a task is defined by its instructions or a "cue." However, the specific cue selection for each task remains largely manual and heuristic. Addressing this, we propose two self-supervised training strategies to automatically adjust LMs for zero-shot performance by optimizing these cue embeddings. In our first method, we define cues as sequences of tokens and refine their representations using cross-entropy loss against the model's predicted class labels. Our second approach represents cues as vectors and updates them via gradient ascent to maximize the model's confidence in the correct class. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art Language Models across tasks from the Natural Language Understanding-Candidate dataset (NLUC-DCC) demonstrate that these methods significantly outperform previous baselines, with the first approach yielding the strongest results.

The two Higgs boson masses detected by the Higgs channel at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) imply a non-standard, or beyond-Standard-Model (BSM), extension. Among various extensions, the Non-Standard-Standard Model (NMSSM) stands out as a minimal framework that simultaneously addresses the hierarchy problem, the nature of dark matter, and electroweak symmetry breaking. This study examines the implications for dark matter and LHC phenomenology under a specific B-breaking NMSSM scenario. We assume vanishing Majorana mass terms for the singlino-glinino sector, single non-zero VEV for the singlet field, and $Z_3$ symmetry. Our findings indicate that this configuration aligns with current experimental data, specifically the Higgs sector measurements and dark matter constraints. We also evaluate the feasibility of detecting gravitational waves from black hole mergers at LIGO-Virgo, focusing on the phase transition dynamics. We determine that an appropriate selection of B-breaking parameters can yield a strong, first-order phase transition, with its strength quantified by the potential's minimum depth. Additionally, we analyze the merger of black holes formed during this phase transition, calculating the associated gravitational wave signals. We find that by adjusting the B-breaking parameters, the model can be made compatible with existing LIGO-Virg observational limits.

We investigate the low-energy dynamical properties of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet situated on a triangular lattice through large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the spin-1/2 susceptibility. By applying a finite-size scaling protocol, we derive a precise description of the inhomogeneous dynamic structure factor across all temperatures, including the quantum regime. Our analysis reveals that the low-energy spectrum comprises three distinct excitations: the standard spin-wave modes found in bipartite systems, a low-energy bulk excitation originating from the formation of local 120$^{\circ}$-bond configurations, and boundary modes located on the surface. Additionally, we examine the nature of the symmetry-breaking order in the classical ground state. Our findings demonstrate that while the standard Néel order is unstable, a novel short-range 120$^{\circ}$-bond ordered phase emerges, characterized by a disruption of the bipartite symmetry. Finally, our numerical results indicate that in a finite two-dimensional system subjected to an external magnetic field, the ground state remains a quantum paramagnetic liquid rather than undergoing a transition to a long-range ordered state.

We investigate the $v=2$ transition in $SU(3)-$Higgs theory, defined by the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry, starting from a model initialized with $SU(3)-$Yang-Mills coupling $g=0$ and adding an isotropic quartic potential $V(\phi) = \lambda/4 Tr(\phi^\dagger phi)^2$. The phase transition is analyzed using Monte Carlo simulations with open boundary conditions, where $v=0$ indicates the symmetric phase and $v=v>0$ signifies symmetry breaking. By varying the coupling parameter $\lambda$ for a fixed $g=0$, we identify a critical value $\lambda_c \approx 0.12$ that marks the boundary between these phases. This finding confirms the existence of the restriction-destriction transition, originally predicted by the strong coupling expansion of the theory. Additionally, our study examines how an $SU(3)-$Yang-Mills interaction with $g>0$ influences this critical coupling $\lambda_c$.

The experimentally measured in-plane magnetic arrangement of Cr2Al, characterized by anisotropic exchange interactions, was investigated using high-precision Monte Carlo simulations. These simulations incorporated exchange parameters derived from first-principles calculations, enabling the determination of anisotropic magnetic susceptibility. Analysis of this calculated susceptibility, obtained through both fit and direct measurement using AC techniques, confirmed the experimental findings. Furthermore, first-principles results indicated that the magnetic susceptibility of Cr2Al is highly sensitive to the degree of exchange anisotropy.

This study introduces a new kinetic model featuring a collision frequency that varies with speed to adequately represent rarefied gas flows influenced by different intermolecular potentials. The model's accuracy was evaluated under various boundary conditions and external force fields through comparisons against the Boltzmann equation and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) methods. Key test cases included thermal creep motion driven by temperature gradients, speed-dependent molecular thermal conductivity under thermal equilibrium, acceleration mechanisms in vacuum chambers caused by rotating walls, and molecular thermal equilibrium acceleration under thermal equilibrium. Additionally, a specific quantitative link was established between the exponent characterizing the molecular potential and the optimal model parameters, demonstrating that the proposed framework is highly flexible and can be precisely tuned for different gases.

We propose a novel approach to develop analyzers that effectively grasp the semantics of previously unseen word types by utilizing extensive pre-training on extensive, general language corpora. Our findings indicate that a fully semantic custom word analyzer built for a specific task requires only a minimal amount of domain-specific data—sufficient to familiarize the model with the essential concepts and structure of that domain—when preceded by pre-training on large, general datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the specific type of pre-training corpus (i.e., the subject matter of pre-learned material) is not critical; rather, the primary determinant of performance is the volume of data used to acclimate the pre-trained model to the target domain's logic and structure.

This study examines the magnetic field structure within HD58260, the most massive star in the Hyades cluster, by analyzing the polarized spectral components of the He I 1083 nm line observed during a spectral line discharge experiment. The findings reveal a nearly linear decrease in the radial magnetic field strength with increasing distance from the stellar surface, where it weakens by a factor of 2.5 at the edge of the chromosphere (approximately 2000 km out). This measured gradient aligns with previous results from similar discharge experiments on other stars and with magnetic inversion models. However, the data also indicate that the corresponding electron discharge current required to generate this field structure would exceed the star's luminosity, suggesting that a simple current layer model cannot fully account for the observed magnetic configuration.

We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line within NGC 5253, a starburst galaxy characterized by low metallicity. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of H30$\alpha$ as a proxy for recent star formation in high-temperature starbursts. The data reveal a compact H30$\alpha$ emission region (0.6 kpc) situated in the galaxy's core, which aligns spatially with a prominent HII region detected via CO observations. Our analysis of the H30$\alpha$ flux yields a Far-UV (FUV) luminosity of 4.2 $\times$ 1$^8$ solar units, corresponding to approximately 1$^3 \times$ 1$^4$ solar units in F$^2$ output. This translates to an estimated star formation rate of roughly 1$^5$ solar units per year. Additionally, the H30$\alpha$ line exhibits significant broadening (FWF = 1$^5$ km/s), indicative of high gas velocities within NGC 5253. We compare these H30$\alpha$-derived star formation metrics with existing measurements based on CO and other tracers to assess their reliability in NGC 5252. The results suggest that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a robust star formation tracer in turbulent, hot starbursts like NGC

In this study, we establish that for a second-countable, compact Hausdorff space $X$ equipped with a continuous action of a Polish group, if the automorphism group of the dynamical system $\mathfrak{X}$ is word-properly, then every automorphism of $\mathfrak{X}$ which is an orbit equivalence to the identity transformation is topologically conjugate to a topologically automorphic transformation of the identity. This result constitutes the definitive solution to the orbit similarity rigidity problem for topologically automorphic groupings, which was previously posed by Pestov and Sauer. The theorem further demonstrates the necessity of the second-countability requirement. Additionally, we demonstrate that if $G$ acts continuously on a Peano space $X$, then every such orbital-conjugate automorphism is also topologically fully conjugate to the identity, thereby fully resolving a query raised earlier by Dodziuk and Pestov.

This work examines the asymptotic properties of the Nadaraya–Watson estimator, which serves as a method for approximating conditional expectation functions. By utilizing a kernel-based approach, the function is defined as the weighted average of Y values, where weights are determined by the proximity of corresponding X values. A key advantage of this nonparametric method is its ability to reveal relationships between X and Y without relying on a priori assumptions regarding the functional form linking them. In contrast to parametric approaches, nonparametric regression may demand larger sample sizes to achieve convergence to the true conditional function. The analysis evaluates the estimator based on two primary properties: its ability to consistently estimate the conditional function as the sample size grows, and its variability. The function is shown to be consistent when the distance parameter h approaches zero as the sample size increases, while the asymptotic variance is derived under a parametric setup. Additionally, the function is compared to its nearest neighbor counterpart, which estimates conditional expectations using values from Y observations closest to a specific X value. The asymptotic characteristics of this alternative method are also investigated.

A novel observer framework is introduced to estimate the dynamic state of epidemic processes. This design incorporates an observer-based testing mechanism to detect anomalies in specific traits; upon detection, a model structure update reconfigures the observer by adapting its mathematical model structures and parameter set. For implementation, mathematical models representing both classic and stochastic SIS and SIR dynamics were constructed, with Linear Observability Analysis conducted to verify their observability. Consequently, to showcase the practical efficacy of this method, the study utilizes data from the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola crisis to estimate and cross-validate the epidemic's state.

Predicting future entities within Knowledge Graphs (KGs) is a critical field driven by the growing complexity of modern KGs and the scarcity of available human and expert annotation for training. While numerous methods exist for static KGs, they are ill-equipped to handle the dynamic nature of temporal KGs, where entities appear, disappear, and reappear over time, often requiring dynamic KG-specific strategies. Conversely, this paper investigates the effectiveness of applying static learning frameworks to temporal KG tasks. Our findings indicate that static models not only perform comparably to or better than current state-of-the-art dynamic methods but also offer superior interpretability. Furthermore, to facilitate reproducibility, we have released code for all evaluated models alongside a curated dataset of five real-world temporal knowledge graphs.

Ultrashort pulse lasers have been crucial for numerous applications, enabling peak powers in the range of gigawatts to terawatts. Mode-locking has been a primary technique for generating these ultrashort pulses since 1965. Over the decades, this method has evolved from simple systems based on Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLKM) to sophisticated setups involving active and passive mechanisms. Despite KLKM's long history and status as a foundational element of ultrafast laser technology, it has recently been revitalized by significant progress in KLKM-based chirped pulse amplification. This resurgence has created a need for a more rigorous, geometric analysis of the technique. This paper provides such a geometric examination of KLKM oscillators operating at gigawatt-level peak powers. It begins by outlining the basics of mode-locking and KLKM before introducing geometric methods. The study utilizes both ray-matrix modeling and geometric modeling to illustrate how these approaches facilitate the design and optimization of KLKM oscillators.

This study addresses online federated learning for nonlinear regression under two key constraints: clients with limited resources and time-varying data availability. To accommodate time-variant data streams, a new asynchronous online federated training framework incorporating an asynchronous alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is proposed. Additionally, a dynamic communication scheduling strategy is developed to enhance the federated online learning approach by considering the time-varying nature of client data streams. The analysis demonstrates that the resulting nonlinear regression estimator is almost surely consistent, and both the computational and communication costs are significantly reduced compared to existing methods.

We introduce a new family of high-dimensional expander (HDX) graphs constructed via group actions on polyhedra. Unlike previously known HDX examples, which often relied on random constructions or connections to finite field geometry and sometimes lacked explicit definitions, our graphs provide a rare, fully explicit model. We demonstrate that these graphs possess the essential characteristics of HDXs, including a spectral gap, robustness against the removal of small sets of vertices, and avoidance of small clique subgraphs. Additionally, we establish a direct relationship between our construction and linear error-correcting codes generated by the transitivity of their respective abelian acting groups. This link enables us to derive novel families of explicit HDXs from existing explicit code families, yielding results ranging from traditional graphs to representations of symmetric and exotic high-dimensional polytopes like the generalized cross-polytopes.

This study examines the magnetic properties of honeycomb lattice GdInO₃, a compound previously identified as a ferromagnet with a low Curie temperature ($T_C \approx 1.5$ K). Contrary to its typical ferro behavior, GdInO₃ was recently detected to exhibit antiferromagnetic characteristics. To resolve the coexistence of both magnetic orders, the authors performed a comprehensive magnetic characterization of GdInO₃, identifying a novel antiferromagnetic phase transition at $N\ell$em $= 1.5$ K. Additionally, GdInO₃ was identified as one of the few oxygen-containing antiferromagnets that remain stable in ambient air.

Link prediction is a critical task in network analysis, particularly for identifying newly formed links in intricate networks. While Significantvectors (SigV) offer a powerful framework for vectorizing link features, they often fail to capture structural network patterns. Addressing this, we introduce Sparse Structural Nets (SSNEvectors), a neural network architecture designed to generate robust representations for both static and dynamic networks. Unlike static versions, our dynamic extension utilizes Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) to process historical data, enabling precise predictions. We assess the SSNEvectors framework using three distinct datasets, demonstrating that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

We present a room-temperature rubidium chamber fabricated from silicon using micro-fabrication techniques for the-ranslation of cold-atom chip-scale technologies. This device, measuring approximately 1.5 cm in length and 0.8 cm in width, incorporates micro-fabricated atomic chambers alongside a laser beam propagation system featuring a 2 mm aperture and a 2 mm-diameter beam waist. The construction process involves deep silicon etching, micro-fabrication, and hermetic sealing with a 2 mm-thick glass plate. These chambers function effectively when paired with a 795 nm diode laser to facilitate 87Rds optical pumping, allowing for the study of inelastic collisions among the vapor atoms. Furthermore, the integration of this compact apparatus with a micro-ring resonator holds significant potential for developing miniaturized, all-optical atomic vapor sensors.

We propose a novel methodology designed to model and measure the nonlinear disturbance power inherent to dual-polarization 4 broadcasting formats comprising single-carrier systems. This approach leverages the relationship between nonlinear distortion power and peak-to-average power ratios (PAPRs) within each polarization plane. By integrating this relationship into a specific calculation formula, the method accurately predicts distortion power for all dual-polarized configurations, regardless of the relative phase or polarization rotation, while significantly reducing computational complexity and accelerating processing speeds. Experimental results demonstrate that the maximum deviation between predictions and actual measurements does not exceed 1.56 dB.

Visible light and infrared (IR) imagery are vital for fire detection, but the latter is frequently constrained by adverse weather conditions. Consequently, integrating both modalities is essential for optimizing detection and monitoring of wildfires. This paper introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel deep deep generative framework designed to fuse visible and IR inputs into a single, realistic output. FIRe-GAN employs a generator and discriminator in an adversarial setup, where the discriminator evaluates realism based on both original training images and those synthetically generated. Notably, the model leverages a one-to-one mapping capability, enabling it to produce a synthetic fusion image for every point in visible data without relying on training-labeled pairs specific to wild fires. Trained on a dataset of visible and IR images from diverse sources, FIRe-GAN was assessed using three metrics: Inception Score (IS), Structural Similarity (SSIM), and Perceptual Similarity. Results demonstrate that the model successfully creates synthetic fire detection imagery that surpasses existing fusion methods. Furthermore, FIRe-GAN was integrated into a deep learning fire classification model, resulting in a 10% absolute increase in accuracy compared to models relying solely on visible or IR inputs.

Depression is a prevalent and severe mental health issue that affects people across all age groups and cultures. Given the rapid expansion of social media usage, users increasingly express their feelings and thoughts online, making these platforms valuable for monitoring public sentiment. However, detecting depression from brief text posts remains difficult due to data privacy concerns and the lack of high-quality datasets. This paper introduces a method for extracting depression indicators from social media content, utilizing a structured data collection pipeline. The proposed system automates the collection process, ensuring consistent adherence to data protection regulations. Furthermore, it implements efficient filtering mechanisms to identify posts indicative of depression, thereby reducing noise. We also present the resulting dataset, the "D2S" (Depression from short-form text Social media), which contains over 1.5 million annotated posts. Empirical evaluations using this dataset demonstrate performance improvements of 30% in the top-ranked systems and a 3% overall gain compared to existing baseline approaches.

**Introduction**
The Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si was investigated using high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy at the National High Magnetic Field Laboratory, utilizing a 245-MeV $^{12}$C beam from the NSCL. The study measured the ISGMR energy, $E_p$, by analyzing the gamma-ray peak centroid following the inelastic $\gamma$-ray de-excitation of the primary $^{24,28}$Si and $^{24}$Al isomers.

**Results**
The $E_p$ values for $^{24}$Mg, $^{28}$Si, and $^{28}$Al were determined to be $(19.2 \pm 0.2)$ MeV, $(19.2 \pm 0.2)$ MeV, and $(19.2 \pm 0.2)$ MeV, respectively. These findings were compared against $E_p$ estimates from three distinct theoretical models: (i) a liquid-drop framework, (ii) a Skyrme-Hartree-Fock approach, and (iii) a relativistic mean-field method.

This study examines how feedback-controlled dynamical systems respond to Coulomb friction, modeled using a discontinuous map where motion transitions between sticking and stick-slip cycles are analyzed via mapping techniques to establish conditions ensuring either convergence to a stuck state or convergence to a periodic orbit. These findings apply to systems governed by both linear and nonlinear friction force feedback mechanisms. The convergence criteria are demonstrated to yield new results regarding damped friction velocity and the standard convergence known for the unregulated case. Ultimately, these conditions find application in the design of feedback controllers capable of preventing stick-slip motion in mechanical systems subject to dry friction.

This work addresses the issue of hedging under model uncertainty within a discrete-time framework. By defining hedging strategies as adapted processes and incorporating a set model specification that permits evaluation by any adapted probability framework, we derive a novel hedging objective known as Bellman hedging. This approach seeks to minimize the aggregate of model deviation penalties and hedging loss costs. We demonstrate that, regardless of the uncertainty quantification method employed, the optimal solution to this problem remains robust across all currently utilized techniques. Furthermore, the optimal solution can be computed efficiently via a dynamic programming procedure that entails minimal computational overhead. Finally, the work establishes asymptotic properties for this method by illustrating convergence results.

Sequential recommenders are designed to forecast the next item a user will select by analyzing their historical interaction sequences. However, the internal driving forces behind these actions remain largely unexplored. This paper introduces a new modeling framework specifically designed to uncover the motivation behind sequence-based interactions. Leveraging our analysis, we developed an enhanced version of a sequential recommender system that integrates motivation awareness to boost performance. Our approach demonstrates strong results on both public benchmarks and datasets collected internally. Additionally, an analysis of our model's representations offers insights into how these learned motivations align with actual user behaviors observed in real-world scenarios.

We introduce efficient methods for approximating a rank-one matrix among blocks of the upper-triangular Cholesky factors derived from complex, multivariate, possibly singular, covariance matrices, where different blocks may vary through distinct vectors and scalars. These blocks often represent covariance matrices from subsets of time-series data exhibiting group-wise heterogeneity. The algorithm utilizes an essential limit theorem to establish the asymptotic distribution of the estimation error, enabling model selection and confidence intervals. Simulations and analyses of financial and neuroimaging data demonstrate that the proposed methodology outperforms prior techniques in accuracy and speed.

Tangents lines to a plane curve form a topological structure in which the mapping from tangents to their contact points is generally not globally continuous, creating new challenges for classical continuum mechanics. This paper examines the mechanics of curves featuring such "topological defects" by modeling them as structures with intrinsic topology rather than relying on explicit symmetry. This approach enables a more accurate representation of curves generated by processes like surface tension, which do not exhibit mirror symmetry. We introduce a model that uniquely determines the orientation of curve segments based on the orientation of the moving tangent line, without requiring a mirror plane. This orientation drives the curve dynamics through a stress tensor derived from curvature and an additional parameter linked to the orientation of the tangles. This framework provides a new physical interpretation for curvature-driven motion, which emerges when the orientating parameter vanishes. Furthermore, we introduce non-curvature stresses that result in a non-trivial boundary interaction between the segment under consideration and its normal direction defined by the tangent line. This mechanism mirrors phenomena observed in the evolution of crystal interfaces driven by anisotropic surface energy.

This research investigates decentralized control architectures designed to enhance both system performance and scalability across large-scale networks. It demonstrates that every large-scale system admits at least one stabilizable and therefore controllable decentralized structure. This paper establishes that for any multi-channel system, a specific number of channels can be added to achieve such a stable and effective structure. This number is bounded above by a value derived from the Schur complement of the Lyapunov matrix, which is itself determined by the system's dynamics. This finding leads to an algorithm capable of identifying a regulation strategy that stabilizes multi-channel networks with minimal interventions. This paper also presents a distributed, algorithm-based approach to regulate linear systems, ensuring that computational overhead scales linearly with the number of components. This method relies on local computations performed by a limited subset of network nodes, utilizing only neighbor-to-neighbor communication. This approach enables the rapid adoption of new devices, thereby facilitating plug-and-play scalability. This method's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a network of 1000 components.

Driven by the rapid global spread of the novel coronavirus, this study introduces a dual-stage categorization framework for the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The initial phase utilizes a pre-trained language model, specifically the 12-layer BERT architecture, to classify collected news articles and social media posts into positive or negative categories. In the second phase, the same BERT model is employed to assign sentiment labels to specific coronavirus-related entities extracted from these texts. By leveraging a recently developed dataset of coronavirus news articles, the research demonstrates that this proposed dual-stage approach for sentiment analysis and entity extraction is more effective than existing conventional methods.

This work serves as an introduction to the field of network science, outlining the fundamental concepts and tools that aspiring network researchers should master. We begin by examining how to model systems as networks, focusing on the distinction between continuous and discrete nodes, as well as directed versus undirected links. Next, we discuss methods for gathering and analyzing both real-world and synthetic data. Our discussion then shifts to structural properties, addressing topological and geometric features of networks along with betweenness and PageRank centrality measures. Following this, we analyze dynamic properties by discussing methods to detect and describe changes within evolving networks. We subsequently examine distribution properties to detail how to calculate and compare various probability distributions across different networks. Finally, we address the challenge of comparing network structures, specifically focusing on graph isomorphism and the problem of network alignment.

The pace at which species adapt to their surroundings fluctuates across history, ranging from ancient epochs to contemporary times. Consequently, modeling these processes requires integrating both historical and contemporary factors. This work presents a unified mathematical framework that simultaneously accounts for the temporal variability in evolutionary dynamics and their dependence on environmental conditions. By employing a master equation, we explore two critical components: first, a stochastic differential equation (SME) that captures fluctuations in selection intensity, and second, a master equation (ME) that models the discrete distribution of mutation rates. Utilizing the noise inherent in these systems, we analyze their combined influence on eco-evolutionary outcomes. Our findings indicate that stochastic fluctuations in evolutionary rates can significantly alter system dynamics, producing effects comparable to those caused by distinct mechanisms of rate variability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fluctuations in the mean evolutionary rate can facilitate the emergence of complex dynamical regimes, such as damped oscillations, sustained cycles, and chaotic behavior. These observations underscore the necessity of incorporating temporal variability into current models to accurately depict real-world eco-evolutionary processes.

Although recent advances in speech self-supervised learning (SSL) have produced effective representations, the potential impact of adversarial speech on these systems remains largely unexamined. This study fills that gap by investigating the vulnerability of both feature extraction and sequence-to-segment models within the SSL framework. Our analysis reveals that while self-supervised pretraining significantly improves robustness against adversarial text-to-speech (TTS) attacks compared to baseline systems, these SSL representations remain susceptible to attacks originating from non-TTS sources. To address this, we introduce a novel defense mechanism based on TTS-to-TTS translation, which demonstrates a substantial improvement in model resilience.

NFTs have rapidly emerged as a major force in the Web3 ecosystem, driving the creation of specialized marketplaces that enable users to effortlessly discover, purchase, and transact digital assets. This surge has attracted the attention of researchers and industry professionals alike, prompting deeper inquiry into the mechanisms governing NFT market dynamics and the specific attributes of these platforms. This overview synthesizes recent research regarding decentralized NFT marketplaces and identifies several promising avenues for future research and development within this field.

This paper introduces a sensitivity analysis approach for handling missing data by adapting the E-value, a metric that quantifies the strength of the confounding association. The resulting methodology allows researchers to determine the upper limit of effect size estimates under various assumptions. We demonstrate the utility of this approach using simulated datasets and a clinical trial dataset involving the drug abacavir, while providing a user-friendly R package to facilitate its application.

While traditional IoT leverages blockchain to ensure security, privacy, and trust, similar advantages make it a natural fit for enhancing IoV services. The new millikelvin cryogenic platform developed at Fermilab's Minimum Temperature Laboratory (MTL) is specifically tailored to satisfy quantum computing's stringent thermal and vibration constraints. The laboratory's temperature is regulated to a stability of 100 µK, while the surrounding room is vibration-isolated with a threshold of 10⁻³ m/s/√Hz. The cryogenic infrastructure features a pulse‑tube precooling chain that extends from 300 K down to 0.7 K, followed by a dilution refrigerator capable of reaching millikelvin levels, all maintained within a vacuum enclosure. The entire facility is automated to minimize human presence, thereby further suppressing anthropogenic vibrations. The research team has fully instrumented the lab and has already conducted initial experiments with a single qubit, while the full quantum processor array experiment is scheduled for completion within the next 12 months.

Labeling large-scale datasets is both a time-consuming and expensive endeavor, particularly within the field of urban scene understanding. While numerous proposed solutions rely on human expertise, they often prove ineffective for tasks involving reasoning, object relationships, or complex contextual analysis. To address this challenge, we introduce an annotating system that utilizes Voting-based Automatic Large-Escale Extensive labeling (VALUE), a system based on collective consensus. In this system, annotators mark points of interest (landmarks) by drawing freehand sketches instead of precise bounding boxes, thereby allowing for a more natural representation of voting patterns across instances. A system based on deep learning trained using these annotated data sets demonstrates remarkable performance in urban environments, achieving state-of-the-art results on City Capstone, the COFO dataset, and the City FLO datasets, demonstrating its potential utility for both large-scale datasets and urban environments.

This work investigates the conformal field theory governing the fixed points of the Haagerup model, an extension of the Ising and Pauli theories. We introduce and apply a novel algorithm for computing the fusion matrix $N_{\sigma \tau}$ via the overlap of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ wavefunctions in the strip. This methodology reveals that finite-size corrections in wavefunction overlaps are strictly determined by the conformal dimensions of the intermediate operators appearing in the strip. Remarkably, this observation holds universally for conformal field theories, transcending specific models. The study of the Haagerup model reveals a non-compact auxiliary sector with a central charge of $c=12$, yet our overlap approach confirms that fusion matrices remain entirely determined by this previously unidentified sector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the wavefunction overlap technique significantly outperforms standard numerical matrix multiplication methods when calculating eigenvectors of the transfer matrix, achieving an order-of-magnitude acceleration.

This work introduces a set-valued part-of-speech (POS) tagging approach designed to enhance the reliability of legacy language corpora, especially those from pre-digital eras where original annotation quality may be questionable. By predicting a set of candidate POS tags for each word rather than selecting a single best fit, this method significantly boosts the recovery of correct annotations without discasing the efficiency required for processing historical data. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system achieves an 86.6% accuracy rate on 18th-century French texts written in a formal register, and a 85.4% rate on 19th-century texts, both of which were originally tagged by a human expert. These findings indicate that employing set-valued prediction enables the accurate tagging of historical materials in a manner that is both highly dependable and reasonably swift.

Building upon Lebesgue theory, this work introduces a new framework for uniformly integrable families of measurable functions by utilizing dual pairs of spaces of measurable real functions equipped with lattice norms. A primary innovation is a novel criterion assessing integral boundedness; notably, in the context of $L^0(X,\mathcal{A},m)$, this criterion relies exclusively on a sequence's behavior in norm rather than on dual elements, marking a distinct divergence from the traditional approach rooted in Dunford-Pettis theorem. Furthermore, we establish essential properties of such non-uniformly integrable sequences, demonstrating the utility of this framework by applying it to two areas previously inaccessible by standard techniques: providing a new demonstration of the generalized Borel-Cantelli lemma and establishing sufficient conditions guaranteeing the almost sure convergence rate of strongly consistent estimators.

Requirements for smart city services are typically captured through a mix of natural language and informal diagrams. In our study, we present a novel, intelligent, and automated approach to interpret these requirements and generate corresponding formal specifications. Our system leverages the Kappa language to define the informal rules found in natural language and the Ka diagram as the formal representation language. By employing an abstract interpretation framework to build a state transition model from a Kappa interpreter, we can translate these simplified requirements into a formal state transition model expressed in Ka. To handle the complexity of processing requirements from a human-centric perspective, we have created a Kappa dialect that utilizes both atomic and high-level constructs for crucial non-functional properties. Additionally, we have developed a Kappa syntax checker integrated with a requirements management tool to facilitate easier use. The paper also outlines a framework for managing requirements, featuring the capability to automatically create, read, and update smart city requirements in a structured and precise manner.

Driven by the escalating difficulty of error correction on quantum devices, we introduce a Concealed Inverses (CI) protocol tailored for such tasks. This approach eliminates the need for specialized, individually decoded inverse gates for all operations within an error correction circuit by relying instead on a universal circuit capable of handling standard operations; it only requires adjustments to specific gates outside the set. To demonstrate its viability, we apply CI to error correction for the S-gate using a superconducting quantum processor, contrasting our results with the traditional method. Our analysis indicates that CI achieves the same fidelity as error correction while generating substantially fewer faults, and experimental verification confirms its superior performance relative to standard techniques.

This study investigates the multivariate spatial conditional extremes of a bivariate Gaussian distribution, where the variables are dependent through a Gaussian correlation coefficient $\rho$ and conditioned on both exceeding a high threshold $u$. As the threshold $u$ tends to infinity, the distributional form of these spatial conditions converges to a new parameterized bivariate distribution termed the Bivariate Gaussian Copula with Spatial Dependence (BGSCD). This new model is characterized by the correlation coefficient $\rho$ and threshold $u$, and it is noted for its tractability, allowing for the analytical calculation of all moments. This paper presents the asymptotic behavior of these multivariate spatial extremes, the development of an estimation method for the parameters, and the derivation of the associated likelihood function. Additionally, we derive a closed-form solution for the probability that at least one variable exceeds threshold $u$ in the context of the derived model. The proposed methodology is then applied to analyze a case study concerning the generation of extreme oceanic weather environments.

Contemporary large-scale contrastive clip models have proven effective for zero-shot generalization by aligning textual and visual embeddings. However, they often fail to capture the visual characteristics implied by text, especially when dealing with complex or abstract capabilities. To address this, we introduce VT-CLIP, a vision-language framework designed to enhance model performance through visual auxiliary assistance. Our strategy involves generating enriched images using multimodal language models (M-LMs) and incorporating these visual enhancements into original images. By feeding these improved versions into CLIP, the resulting alignment between visual and textual embeddings becomes more precise, effectively reducing the reliance on textual prompts to carry complex concepts. Consequently, we observe significant enhancements in CLIP's zero-shot capabilities across various tasks.

We present a generalization of the operator transitioning framework originally proposed by Chen et al. (2018), extending its utility beyond stochastic methods to various undirected noisy optimization frameworks. This approach allows for the analysis of a broad class of undirected Markov chains, providing theoretical guarantees for an accelerated convergence rate of $O(\sigma^2 \log^2(\varepsilon^{-1}))$, where the parameter $\sigma$ characterizes the convergence speed of the underlying chain. Our findings demonstrate that the original operator transitioning technique serves as a special case within this new, comprehensive framework. We validate the method's effectiveness through applications to the analysis of Chen et al.'s (2018) original approach, as well as to the matrix setting of accelerated proximal gradient descent and proximal point algorithms operating over a product space of convex functions.

The authors demonstrate that for an Artinian local $(R, m)$ ring with a linear Hilbert polynomial, the $F$-invariant holds if and only if the socle degree of $R/\mathfrak q$ is tight for every parameter ideal $\{\mathfrak q\}$. Additionally, necessary and sufficient conditions are provided to determine when a standard graded algebra $A = S/I$ is $F$-invariant, assuming its Hilbert polynomial is linear. Specifically, the $A$ ring exhibits $F$-invariance precisely when the socle degree of its $G$ associated ring's parameter sequences is consistently tight. The analysis further establishes that for Artinian $\mathbb N$-invariant local rings $(R,m)$ with residue field $\mathbb k$ of characteristic $p>2$, and the associated graded ring $G(R)$ generated by a minimal system of parameters, the ring $R$ is $F$-invariant provided the socle degree of $G(R)$'s $M$ associated $R/m$-module is always within the range $[d-1, 2]$.

Image analysis has become a cornerstone of machine learning within medical imaging; however, developing models for whole slide images necessitates vast datasets comprising gigabytes of slide data alongside corresponding interpretation text. Although imaging biomarkers are common in conventional radiology, quantifying these images often struggles to find a standardized format for their precise communication. Highdicom offers a comprehensive, scalable solution for encoding image data and metadata using the DICOM PS3.3 standard, a widely adopted protocol for medical device interoperability. By streamlining the exchange of detailed quantitative results, the tool supports standardized communication workflows for clinical use.

This work investigates the nonlinear asymptotic symmetries inherent in general relativity when paired with an Einstein-Hilbert action that includes a boundary term. By employing the Noether charge strategy, the boundary dynamics reveal an infinite-dimensional symmetry group isomorphic to the product of two Virasoro groups. Applying Brown and Henneaux's central extension formula yields a non-central, finite central extension that matches general relativity without a boundary term in its leading order but features a specific value for the central charge in its subleading term. This term is directly proportional to the cosmological constant and becomes identical to the product of two infinite-dimensional, global isometry groups represented by $ISO(3,1)$. Subsequent analysis of the spectrum generated by these symmetries demonstrates that the quantum states follow a finite temperature thermal distribution. The study also explores the physical significance of a spatially dependent disorder parameter within the bulk action, linking it to holographic entanglement entropy calculations and establishing a relationship with the spectrum's temperature. Furthermore, the text addresses the physical meaning of this spatially varying disorder from a quantum information standpoint.

Although numerous research studies have explored the bioinformatics domain, the majority depend on feature engineering guided by existing biological knowledge. This approach is not only extremely time-consuming but also frequently fails to yield optimal results. In this work, we introduce a novel methodology for deriving feature representations of DNA sequences. We first formulate a representation system that maps DNA sequences into real-valued vectors and then leverage a matrix factorization approach to generate sequential matrix representations, ultimately extracting gene-related features via attention mechanisms tailored for genomic data. We validate this method using single-cell RNA-Seq data to perform unsupervised clustering of genes and DNA-binding proteins, revealing highly promising outcomes.

The vanadium (V) atoms in these films were probed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). We found a $\sim$0.5 eV shift in the MIT temperature between the thinner and bulkier samples. This work presents the introduction of Clibsch functions defined on Lie-Poisson linear systems that yield constant invariants. While these functions vary with specific system parameters and are generally not Poisson, they serve a vital role: authorizing integrable sets of Lie-Poisson linear dynamics via the method of involution. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for identifying these Clibsch functions and provide algorithmic steps to locate them. To demonstrate the method, we examine two cases: a space-charge swing oscillator and the dynamics of a magnetized particle within an anisotropic undulator field.

We present the findings of the most comprehensive and efficient survey to date for identifying exoplanetary systems with irregular orbits, utilizing a systematic search through the KMT2018 dataset of sub-pixel anomalies. This study focuses on binaries exhibiting orbital periods shorter than the target project duration but showing a mismatch with integer fractions of the fundamental frequency. The researchers analyzed a sample of 1,018 candidate pairs, of which 101 were confirmed as false alarms, leaving a verified inventory of 916 systems that exhibit no evidence of orbital periodicity. Among these confirmed non-periodic binaries, 106 have confirmed exoplanet hosts. We detect a clear trend where detection rates correlate with the known occurrence of planets, rising from 16% in the cases of known planets to 45% in the cases of non-exoplanet hosts. Additionally, we observe that irregular systems tend to possess longer remaining lifespans than the average population, suggesting that eccentric orbits are less likely to result in orbital decay over time. We also provide a full catalog for the sub-pixel anomaly dataset, which includes the positions, coordinates, and classifications for all binary systems identified in this study.

In the second part of this series, we present specific instances of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations that incorporate the fundamental tenets of conservation management. For a designated sub-domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ ($N \geq 2$), let $n$ represent the population density and $u$ represent the average velocity of the group. Under the assumption of significant competition within the domain, the principle of conservation management dictates that $n$ must adhere to the inequality $0 \leq n \leq K$, where $K$ is a constant carrying specific significance. The analysis focuses on the weak solution of a fundamental Navier-Stokes equation modified with such a constraint, initially establishing the existence of solutions through the approximation method. Subsequently, an upper bound for the Reynolds number is identified to guarantee the existence of a Navier-Stokes solution with bounded derivatives.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for analyzing creditworthiness using machine learning on the NPL (Non-Performing Loan) dataset. We conducted an extensive evaluation of algorithms, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and Deep Neural Networks, alongside a rigorous feature significance analysis. The core methodology employs Bayesian optimization to automatically tune hyperparameters, ensuring optimal model performance. This study examines the mass of the top quark using two mass definitions, $m_{\rm pole}$ and $\bar{m}_Q(\mu)$, both possessing substantial flavor and scale dependencies. The results indicate that the top quark exhibits a strong dependence on the underlying flavor in the $\bar{m}_Q(\mu)$ framework, particularly at lower values of $\mu$. This work introduces a novel edge-dyeing algorithm capable of assigning unique, positive integer labels to every edge of a graph $G$ such that the absolute difference between the colors of adjacent edges at any node $v$ produces distinct values. The algorithm proceeds sequentially, moving from one edge to the next via an optimal path that depends solely on the current edge set and existing colors. For graphs $G$ that are nearly regular (defined as regular except for at most one irregular vertex), the maximum color assigned does not exceed the number of edges $m$ by one. Theoretically, the algorithm requires at most $O(m^2)$ steps to execute. In recent years, there has been a significant increase in the use of deep learning for medical image analysis, particularly in the domain of computer-aided detection (CAD) for pneumonia. While low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) scans are currently the primary tool for identifying this respiratory disease, the urgent deployment of a new CAD system became evident at the onset of COVID-19 due to the lack of rapid diagnostic methods. Consequently, a novel two-stage network was proposed to address the dual challenges of distinguishing COVID-19 from other conditions and the high false-positive rates associated with typical signs of fluid accumulation in LDCT images. This study investigates the spatial availability of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) for future satellite deployments. Employing a specific LEO model to assess critical parameters, we examine both the physical environment and the usable volume considering constraints such as radiation, debris, and density limits. Our analysis further explores how these factors are interdependent in defining LEO capacity. Additionally, we apply various metrics to quantify orbital capacity, highlighting the interplay among these measures using LEO satellite constellation examples. The discussion addresses the implications of congestion within LEO, including the risks posed by existing debris and the resulting challenges for launch planning and operations.

This paper presents a novel approach to generating a coarse, high-order element grid within CAD models. An integer linear optimization framework is employed to position grid corner points directly on the surface of CAD geometry, ensuring that the resulting grid elements maintain conformity with curved surfaces and the geometry's global symmetry. Grid alignment with tangential surfaces and proper orientation of grid normals are also prioritized. Subsequently, a fine, high-order mesh is automatically generated over these refined coarse grids. The method is demonstrated on several complex aerospace structures, yielding coarse grids that significantly outperform those produced by current state-of-the-art commercial tools in terms of element size, with automated generation of the subsequent fine mesh.

Moment-based approaches are essential tools for examining data and are fundamental to many widely used statistical methods. In this study, we concentrate on the sample correlation, which is a fundamental metric for quantifying the degree of linear association between two variables. Given its prevalence, we derived precise formulas for the mean and variance of the sample correlation calculated over all possible samples of size $n$ from datasets with $p$ features in $\mathbb{R}^p$. Additionally, we provided corresponding formulas regarding the sample correlation's median. To the best of our knowledge, these analytical results represent the first of their kind and enable rapid computation, thereby rendering their computational application feasible even for ranges of features previously considered too large.

Furthermore, we analyze a previously proposed method for constructing gravitational EFTs that relies on the equivalence between relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum field theory.
