However, constructing and deploying these models often demands substantial effort and specific expertise, particularly when the need arises to frequently adapt them to new requirements or expand their capabilities to accommodate fresh data sources. This work presents MMLSpark, a scalable deep learning framework integrated within the Apache Spark ecosystem, which enables data scientists to swiftly build, customize, and scale up learning algorithms. By leveraging the extensive distributed computing resources and robust data processing tools provided by MMLSpark and Apache Spark, researchers and practitioners can effectively manage a broad spectrum of tasks, from model refinement and new data integration to cross-platform deployment of these updated algorithms.

Voice translation, a core element of multilingual speech communication, is currently hindered by the need for source-domain fine-tuning and extensive parallel corpora. In this work, we tackle the zero-shot voice translation challenge, which demands translating audio from a source language into a target language without any specific training data. Our proposed method, named zero-shot TVT, utilizes a unified architecture that integrates speech synthesis and recognition. This approach infers voice translation by first generating the acoustic output of a spoken sentence and then determining its meaning through a meaning representation, effectively decoupling the process. Additionally, we introduce a novel unsupervised data augmentation technique that leverages existing voice translation systems to refine the performance of unsupervised models. Experimental results demonstrate that our system significantly outperforms other zero-shot methods, achieving a reduction of over 10 BLEU in loss metrics and surpassing state-of-the-art fine-tuned approaches by approximately 2 BLEU in loss.

This study examines a thermal model characterized by the first-order spatial derivative in the heat equation, dynamic boundary conditions, and new Coleman-Gurtin type equations incorporating lower and upper thermal bounds alongside dynamic relaxations. We demonstrate the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of weak and strong solutions for this system.

The increasing adoption of distributed generation and distributed energy storage systems necessitates accurate load forecasting to mitigate grid impacts. This paper introduces a probabilistic framework for predicting daily peak loads and their distributions at the low-voltage level, utilizing a data-driven approach. A key innovation lies in the new fusion method for combining daily peak forecasts derived from two distinct sources: historical data and high-fidelity physical models. The specific objectives are to (i) generate probabilistic daily peak load profiles for a LV network, (2) create robust forecasting tools to manage the operational challenges posed by LV distribution, and 3) validate the robustness and accuracy of the proposed algorithms through a practical case study.

We introduce a structured framework for embedding domain expertise within machine learning (ML) initiatives. Recognizing that a vast and rapidly evolving body of knowledge surrounds every ML-impacted field, our approach offers a systematic method to guide specialists in effectively conveying their insights to data scientists. We outline four strategic levels for expertise integration, providing distinct advantages and potential challenges at each. Additionally, we propose a unified taxonomy of domain expertise that fills the void left by existing taxonomies, which are either too narrow or too broad for practical utility. Finally, we illustrate this blueprint through applications in both healthcare and sports domains.

The ongoing global pandemic has severely impacted the worldwide economy and society, driving extensive research into its mitigation. Medical imaging-based lesion localization and segmentation have become vital tools for monitoring and treating infectious diseases, including COVID-19. However, the scarcity of detailed annotated data and inherent model biases pose significant obstacles to developing impartial and precise segmentation systems. This paper introduces the Weakly Guided training strategy to the Lesion Localization and Segmentation (LUL) task. We first develop an automatic dataset annotation method that reduces manual labeling effort by 90%. Subsequently, we apply the proposed Weakly Guided learning (WGL) technique to overcome data bias and enhance LUL performance. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving improvements of 10.6% in Dice similarity coefficient and 10.59 dB in Peak Signal-to-Nale Ratio for segmentation accuracy. Additionally, the code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhenguo99/WGL_Segmentation.

Although the brain is central to the human body, the spine is critical for supporting the soft tissues and muscles that enable movement. Degenerative diseases affecting the spine are a leading cause of chronic pain and disability, driving the need for precise diagnosis and treatment planning. However, the process of manually localizing vertebrae and assessing their condition from CT images is highly time-consuming, typically requiring 10–20 minutes per scan. To address this, we introduce a learning-based method for automatically localizing and classifying vertebrae, which involves training a regression model to align unrectified CT images into anatomically correct views. This rectification significantly enhances localization accuracy by accounting for CT scanning irregularities. We further employ a voxel-based neural network to predict the anterior and posterior vertebral body boundaries and five key anatomical landmarks. Additionally, we develop an anatomically constrained optimization framework that refines the localization and classification of vertebral levels and pathologies, yielding state-of-the-art results on the L vertebra dataset with an average localization error of just 1.50 voxels.

We present a numerical investigation of how dynamical stabilization influences the multi-photon ionization of a hydrogen atom driven by a strong laser field confined within a cavity. Using a time-dependent numerical approach, we examine how dynamical stabilization behaves under varying strong-coupling conditions defined by different cavity sizes. Our findings indicate that changing the cavity dimensions significantly alters the atom's response to the field. Notably, a new phenomenon emerges in small cavities: the formation of a specific standing wave pattern that leads to local intensity peaks precisely at the core of the atom. This results in the suppression of electron oscillations and the concurrent experimental or numerical enhancement of dynamical stabilization. Furthermore, this ultrastrong interaction regime between light and matter enables the observation of resonant electron scattering events.

While electric actuators are standard in current walking robots, they are often complemented by elastic components to enhance efficiency and resilience. Nevertheless, simulating the nonlinear dynamics of these soft, elastic systems poses significant modeling challenges. This study introduces a reinforcement learning framework that automatically identifies and exploits the optimal elasticity within quadrupedal systems, as measured by specific actuator parameters. Our approach addresses the complexity introduced in quadrupedal locomotion by leveraging symmetry to reduce state space dimensions and by using elastic energy as part of the reward signal. We evaluate this method against both a soft-robot baseline and a control-based technique that incorporates foot placement information. The findings demonstrate that the proposed strategy effectively targets and uses the system's inherent softness, resulting in superior performance in both running and climbing compared to the competing methods.

This work introduces a variational approach to resolve the issue of quantum distinguishability. By applying a functional that optimizes subspaces for optimal discrimination, we demonstrate that the distinguishability of states is not solely determined by their distance, but also depends on their temporal evolution and initial conditions. Consequently, distinguishability can be enhanced through two mechanisms: increasing the separation between state vectors or introducing a broader class of initial conditions. Furthermore, we establish a direct link between the optimized distinguishability of states and their quantum relative entropy, while also deriving the analytical form of the corresponding optimal measurement strategy.

Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental process in astrophysical plasmas, though the specific mechanisms driving reconnection in collisionless plasmas remain debated. This study investigates the tearing instability within a collisionless slab plasma, specifically examining the role of anisotropic velocity distributions. By implementing a drift kinetic approach, we demonstrate that magnetic curvature drives the growth of tearing modes, while anisotropic velocity distributions establish the initial width of the reconnection region. Through self-consistent particle-in-cell simulations, we confirm this proposed mechanism and visualize the resulting reconnection dynamics.

Feature-based trait manipulation (TLT) is a recent approach designed to handle fashion image retrieval (FIR). It functions by converting an input image into a compact set of features, which are then assigned to specific nodes in a tree structure. Each node represents a specific clothing item and includes a set of features with corresponding weights. The final representation is generated by aggregating these weighted features. While effective, this method relies heavily on large volumes of labeled data, creating significant barriers for training on fIR tasks where labeled data is hard to acquire. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a semi-supervised framework that enables training with minimal labeled and numerous unlabeled images. Our approach features a weighted contrastive learning (WCL) framework that leverages both individual feature similarities and overall image-level similarities to guide learning. Furthermore, we propose a dynamic adjustment mechanism to regulate the influence of weights during training. Experimental results on the PolyFASHION and MetaFASHION benchmarks confirm that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques specifically in the domain of label-scarce, labeled-semi-supervised FIR retrieval.

We introduce a framework for addressing an extensive range of linear ill-posed problems within the functional setting of Banach spaces, utilizing a dual gradient descent approach. Unlike the well-established primal gradient methods that rely on regularization and require the strong separability of the space, our methodology functions effectively even when these classical prerequisites are absent, particularly for spaces lacking a separated dual. Moreover, this approach is versatile enough to encompass various regularized least squares formulations, ranging from Tikhonov to those incorporating $\ell_1$, Bregman, or norm penalties. Crucially, convergence rates are derived contingent upon the smoothness properties of the target solution, with the theoretical results demonstrated for both separable and non-separable Banach spaces.

We introduce an innovative application for light field (LF) depth estimation that addresses two primary hurdles: generating synthetic occlusion boundaries and accounting for variable view angles during the rendering process. Traditional methods typically rely on segmentation-based techniques to handle occlusion, a strategy that proves inefficient in this context. Instead, we propose an occlusion-aware system that models occlusion borders directly within the synthesized view, eliminating dependence on separate occlusion masks. Our approach further integrates multiview rendering to utilize angular cues for reconstructing depth along object boundaries. Empirical results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing state-of-the-art LF depth estimation techniques, delivering both higher accuracy and improved speed.

This study establishes the bilinear Lax–Plei formula associated with the Fokas–Lenells equation. By introducing a set of specific bilinear identities, the authors derive the complete 1–N soliton solutions. The paper provides explicit expressions of a few key bilinear identities and the associated binary operators. Furthermore, the binary operators are utilized to demonstrate binary integrable properties of the Fokas–Lenells equation.

Non-Riemannian frames have recently been explored within geometric approaches to gravity, notably within the 3+1 formalism, where they yield novel field equations alongside new degrees of freedom capable of describing cosmological dynamics. Double field theory (DFT), a unifying framework for string gravity, has recently facilitated the development of a general action formula: $S=\int d^{D}x\sqrt{-g}G$, where $G$ represents an effective scalar curvatures. In this study, we present a class of such actions rooted in DFT that describe various non-Riemannian theories. By performing expansions of these actions in non-orthonormal metric variables, we identify that these actions consistently generate second-order differential equations for every degree of freedom. We further demonstrate that our framework encompasses the Einstein-Hilbert and Riemannian Horndeski actions, as well as a broader class of non-Riemannian Horndeski-type actions, within its structure.

In multi-point IEEE 802.11 networks, interference arises from APs operating on the same channel, while signal coverage gaps are often addressed by deploying range extender devices. This paper introduces two novel IEEE 802.11 protocols, specifically an and ' to enable user devices to assess the loading levels of nearby APs. By measuring local and nearby load, these new protocols allow user devices to make intelligent selection decisions for both primary APs and range extenders. The proposed measurement mechanism is an enhancement of the Neighbor Report found in the 802.11k protocol, while is a new protocol that facilitates the selection of nearby signal amplification points based on real-time load analysis. These protocols are compatible with current IEEE 802.11 standards, requiring no new frame structures, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing wireless local area networks. The paper presents the fundamental mechanisms, provides detailed protocols, and includes an analysis of the system's performance.
